category: Fused relatives, generic pronouns, and dummy pronouns

entries.meaning: 'All those that' — the plural fused relative, and the one that takes a plural verb.
examples: As many as want to come are welcome to come.
Take as many as you need — there's a whole case of them in the back.
As many as received the notice have already written back.
We carried out as many as we could before the smoke got bad.
The clause binds as many as sign it, and nobody else. (contract boilerplate, and the archaic use)
As many as were present that evening still remember the noise.
The headline said as many as forty flights were canceled — a count in front of a numeral, not a pronoun.

senses.head: All those that (fused relative)
body: The archaic core, alive in scripture and in formal drafting: As many as were willing came forward. 2. As many as you need. The everyday use, where the as-clause sets a limit instead of naming a set: Take as many as you want. 3. Not this word at all. As many as forty people is a degree modifier standing in front of a numeral, and no pronoun is involved.
examples: As many as want to come are welcome to come.
Take as many as you need — there's a whole case of them in the back.
As many as received the notice have already written back.
We carried out as many as we could before the smoke got bad.
The clause binds as many as sign it, and nobody else. (contract boilerplate, and the archaic use)
As many as were present that evening still remember the noise.
The headline said as many as forty flights were canceled — a count in front of a numeral, not a pronoun.

entries.pronunciation note: both instances of as are ordinarily weak /əz/, so the phrase runs to [əz ˈmɛni əz] with the only real accent on man-; the first as recovers its full /æz/ only under contrastive stress. many keeps its /n/ in every register — there is no reduction to ✗ [ˈmɛi]
entries.русский: столько, сколько; все те, кто — берёт множество целиком; глагол во мн. ч.
entries.case: none — one invariant form for subject and object
entries.register: split. The "all those who" use is archaic, biblical, and formal, and an American meets it in scripture, in older prose, and in contract boilerplate; the everyday take as many as you need is neutral and unremarkable
entries.type: fused relative pronoun — the plural member of the group
entries.person / number: third person, invariant in form, and plural for agreement — the only fused relative in this file that is.
entries.refers to: the whole set that satisfies the clause — people (as many as were willing) or things (as many as we could carry). Unlike whoever it is not restricted to people, and unlike whatever it is not restricted to things; what it does insist on is that the set be countable and plural. For a mass quantity the phrase is as much as.
entries.agreement: plural verb — As many as want to come are welcome, ✗ As many as wants to come is welcome. This is the single agreement exception in the fused-relative group, and it comes from many, which is plural by nature. Compare the singular whoever, which says the same thing one person at a time: Whoever wants to come is welcome.
entries.pattern: as many as [plural verb] — as subject, as many as were present signed it · [verb] as many as [subject] [verb] — as object, take as many as you need · [preposition] as many as [clause] · as many as [subject] want / like / need / can carry · the counting frame as many as [numeral] [noun] — not this pronoun
entries.contrast: two constructions share the spelling and only one of them is here. As a pronoun it fills a noun slot and means "all those that": As many as received the notice have already replied. As a degree modifier it stands in front of a number and means "up to, and surprisingly so": As many as forty people were turned away — nothing there is filling a noun slot, the numeral is, and that use belongs with the quantifiers. The test is substitution: if all those who or all the ones that drops in cleanly, it is the pronoun. Against whoever, the difference is number and range — whoever is singular and people only, as many as is plural and takes things as well. Against as much as, the difference is count against mass: as many as you need of chairs, as much as you need of coffee. Against such as (fused relative), which is the same archaic move made with such — such as were present is the older sibling of as many as were present. And put a noun straight behind it (as many as fifty applicants) and it has stopped being a pronoun altogether.
entries.variants: as many standing alone with the clause understood (take as many), the mass counterpart as much as, and the archaic sibling such as
entries.see also: whoever, whatever, whichever, what (fused relative), as, such as (fused relative), as much, many, many

entries.term: he who, he that, she who, they that
entries.meaning: 'Anyone who' — the antecedent and the relative kept as two separate words, the way English said it before whoever fused them.
examples: He who hesitates is lost. (a frozen proverb, quoted rather than produced)
He that hath ears to hear, let him hear. (King James Bible, with the archaic -th inside the clause)
Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.
The prize goes to him who finishes first. (split case: object of to, subject of finishes; modern English to whoever finishes first)
She who must be obeyed has already decided where we are eating. (jocular archaism)
They that sow in tears shall reap in joy. (plural antecedent, plural verb)
In a new policy, write those who apply late, not he who applies late.

senses.head: The proverb frame
body: Quoted whole rather than built fresh: He who hesitates is lost. 2. Scripture and hymn. He that hath ears to hear, let him hear. 3. Deliberate archaism. A modern writer reaching for weight or for a joke: she who must be obeyed. 4. The split-case form. him who, him that — antecedent in the object case, relative still a subject.
examples: He who hesitates is lost. (a frozen proverb, quoted rather than produced)
He that hath ears to hear, let him hear. (King James Bible, with the archaic -th inside the clause)
Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.
The prize goes to him who finishes first. (split case: object of to, subject of finishes; modern English to whoever finishes first)
She who must be obeyed has already decided where we are eating. (jocular archaism)
They that sow in tears shall reap in joy. (plural antecedent, plural verb)
In a new policy, write those who apply late, not he who applies late.

entries.pronunciation note: the antecedent keeps its full /hi/ because it opens the phrase and carries a beat, and who, which takes the phrase accent, keeps its full /hu/; the word that reduces is that, so he that is ordinarily [hi ðət] with weak /ðət/ and he that hath runs to [hi ðət ˈhæθ]. she who /ʃi ˈhu/ shee-HOO, he that /hi ˈðæt/ hee-THAT, they that /ðeɪ ˈðæt/ thay-THAT with weak they [ðe]. The w of who has been silent for centuries, so the word begins with a plain /h/
entries.русский: тот, кто; та, кто; те, кто — устар., книжн.; в новой прозе заменено на whoever
entries.case: split — the antecedent takes the case of the outer clause (he, object him), the relative takes the case of the inner one (who, object whom)
entries.register: archaic; alive in proverbs, scripture, hymns, and deliberate formality. An American meets it in the King James Bible, in maxims, and in nineteenth-century prose, and essentially never in new writing
entries.type: antecedent pronoun plus relative pronoun — the two-word ancestor of the fused relative, entered here beside the forms that replaced it
entries.person / number: third person; he who, she who, and he that are singular, they that and they who plural.
entries.refers to: a person defined by the clause that follows — "anyone who," "the one who." He who was the traditional generic and now reads as generic masculine, which is why edited American prose has replaced it with whoever, anyone who, or those who; she who names a woman, or is used deliberately as a rhetorical counterweight.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the antecedent pronoun: singular with he who, she who, and he that — He who hesitates is lost — and plural with they that and they who — They that sow in tears shall reap in joy. Older texts carry the archaic inflection inside the relative clause: he that hath ears, she that doeth good.
entries.pattern: he who [verb] … [main verb] · he that [verb] · [verb or preposition] him who [verb] — the split-case form, give it to him who asks · she who [verb] · they that [verb] · the frozen proverb frames He who hesitates…, He who laughs last…
entries.contrast: this is the construction whoever replaced, and setting them side by side shows what fusion bought. He who keeps the two case jobs in two separate words, so the outer clause can pull the antecedent into the object case while the relative stays a subject: Give it to him who asks — him is the object of to, who the subject of asks. Whoever has one word for both jobs and settles it on the inner clause alone: Give it to whoever asks, never ✗ to whomever asks. Against those who: that is the modern plural replacement and what an American editor now reaches for, since it carries no masculine default. Against that which: the same shape for things instead of people. He which was ordinary in 1611 (Our Father which art in heaven) and is a plain error today — for a person the relative is who or that. And the case inside the clause is still read off that clause: in he who I met, the relative is the object of met, so a frame this deliberately archaic wants he whom I met for consistency of register. Be exact about what that is — object who is standard American English everywhere else (see whom), so this is a register slip inside an antique construction, not a grammatical error. In ordinary English the whole thing is the man I met.
entries.variants: he that, she that, they who, him who, him that, and the single-word archaisms whoso and whosoever
entries.see also: whoever, whomever, whosoever, he (generic), those who, that which, whoso

entries.meaning: 'The thing that' — a noun phrase and its relative clause fused into a single word.
examples: What I need right now is about ten hours of sleep.
She got exactly what she paid for.
What happened at the meeting is still not clear to me.
Just tell them what you told me.
That is not what I meant, and you know it.
He never spends what he earns.
What worries the committee is the cost of the second phase.

senses.head: The thing(s) that
body: The core use: the clause names a thing without ever naming it. 2. The pseudo-cleft. Fronting a what-clause and parking the news at the end (What I need is coffee) is one of the main ways English moves emphasis, and it is why so many spoken sentences begin with What I'm saying is… or What happened was…
examples: What I need right now is about ten hours of sleep.
She got exactly what she paid for.
What happened at the meeting is still not clear to me.
Just tell them what you told me.
That is not what I meant, and you know it.
He never spends what he earns.
What worries the committee is the cost of the second phase.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /wət/, and the t flaps into a following vowel, so what I need runs to [wəɾ aɪ ˈnid] and what's to [wəts]. Conservative and many Southern speakers keep an /hw-/ onset: /hwʌt/
entries.русский: то, что — содержит собственный антецедент; только о предметах, не о людях
entries.case: none — one invariant form for subject and object
entries.register: neutral
entries.person / number: third person, invariant. The what-clause counts as singular for agreement.
entries.refers to: things, substances, ideas, events, and whole situations — never to a specific person. For people use whoever. The complement of a pseudo-cleft may still name people (What we need is more nurses), because what names the need, not the nurses.
entries.agreement: a subject what-clause takes a singular verb by default — What matters is the deadline, ✗ What matter is the deadline. In the pseudo-cleft the copula is singular by default too (What I need is a vacation); before a plural complement both What we need is more volunteers and What we need are more volunteers are current in educated American English and neither is worth correcting. The verb inside the clause goes plural only when the clause is itself plainly plural, which in practice means with a linking or raising verb in it: What appear to be errors are actually rounding differences.
entries.pattern: what [subject] [verb] — as clause subject · [verb] what [subject] [verb] — as object · [preposition] what [clause] · What [clause] is [phrase] — the pseudo-cleft · [phrase] is what [clause] — the reverse pseudo-cleft
entries.nonstandard: what as a plain relative pronoun — the man what fixed the roof — is regular in London and other British vernaculars and in Southern, Appalachian, and rural American speech, and it is rule-governed there; it is not standard written English. Its entry is what (nonstandard relative).
entries.contrast: what means "the thing(s) that," so it must never sit on top of an antecedent: ✗ the thing what I need — write either the thing that I need or what I need, never both. That is exactly what separates it from relative that and which, which require an antecedent already standing in the sentence. Against interrogative what, the test is whether an answer is being requested: I know what he wants reports a thing, I asked what he wants embeds a question.
entries.see also: whatever, whoever, it (extraposition), which, what (relative determiner), what (interrogative)

entries.meaning: 'Anything that,' with no limit put on the range.
examples: Take whatever you need from the supply closet.
Whatever she decides, the rest of us will go along with it.
He believes whatever the last person told him.
Whatever is left over goes home with you.
I'll pay whatever it costs to get the car back on the road.
They can call it whatever they like; it's still a tax.

senses.head: Anything that (fused relative)
body: Fills a noun slot in the sentence. 2. No matter what (concessive). An adverbial clause, normally fronted and followed by a comma. 3. Dismissal. Standalone Whatever. means "I decline to argue" — informal, and read as rude in most workplaces.
examples: Take whatever you need from the supply closet.
Whatever she decides, the rest of us will go along with it.
He believes whatever the last person told him.
Whatever is left over goes home with you.
I'll pay whatever it costs to get the car back on the road.
They can call it whatever they like; it's still a tax.

entries.pronunciation note: the t is a flap in ordinary speech, so it comes out [wəˈɾɛvɚ]; the accent sits on -ev-, never on what-
entries.русский: всё, что; что бы ни — о вещах; разг. отдельное Whatever. — «да пофиг»
entries.case: none — invariant
entries.register: neutral; the standalone dismissive Whatever. is informal only
entries.type: fused relative pronoun, and concessive pronoun
entries.person / number: third person, invariant, treated as singular.
entries.refers to: things and situations, with the range left open — "anything at all that." Not people (use whoever). In the concessive use its scope can be a whole clause.
entries.agreement: singular verb — Whatever is left goes in the fridge, ✗ Whatever are left. Even where the sense is plainly plural, the verb stays singular: Whatever remains is yours.
entries.pattern: whatever [verb] — as subject · [verb] whatever [subject] [verb] — as object · [preposition] whatever [clause] · Whatever [clause], [main clause] — concessive, comma required
entries.contrast: two distinct jobs, and the comma tells them apart. As a fused relative it fills a noun slot: I'll eat whatever you cook (object of eat). As a concessive it is an adverbial sitting outside the main clause and paraphrasable as "no matter what": Whatever you cook, I'll eat it. Against whichever: whatever leaves the range open (take whatever you want — anything at all), whichever picks from a set already on the table (take whichever you want — one of these). Spaced what ever is a third thing entirely, an intensified question: What ever were you thinking? And the emphasizer in no evidence whatsoever is not this pronoun — nor, strictly, a determiner: it is a postposed negative-polarity emphasizer belonging to the noun phrase, which is why it stands after the noun and never in the determiner slot (see whatsoever (determiner)).
entries.see also: what (fused relative), whichever, whoever, whatsoever, whatever (determiner)

entries.meaning: 'Anything at all that' — the emphatic, archaic form of whatever.
examples: Whatsoever ye do, do it heartily.
The trustee may sell, lease, or mortgage whatsoever belongs to the estate.
Whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
He was authorized to do whatsoever the board directed.
The license covers whatsoever the artist produces during the term.
Whatsoever is not of faith is sin.
entries.pronunciation note: main accent on -ev-, secondary on what-; the middle syllable is a full /soʊ/, not a reduced one
entries.русский: всё, что бы то ни было — устар., библ., юр. усиленное whatever
entries.case: none — invariant
entries.register: archaic, biblical, and legal
entries.person / number: third person, invariant, singular for agreement.
entries.refers to: things and actions, with maximal scope — "anything at all that." Not people; the corresponding forms there are whosoever and whomsoever.
entries.agreement: singular verb — Whatsoever is written here is binding. Older texts keep the archaic inflection to match (whatsoever he doeth).
entries.pattern: Whatsoever [subject] [verb], [main clause] · [verb] whatsoever [subject] [verb] · [preposition] whatsoever [clause]
entries.contrast: identical in meaning to whatever and differing only in emphasis and in age. The one place whatsoever is thoroughly alive in modern American English is after a negated noun — no reason whatsoever, none whatsoever — and there it is not a pronoun at all but a postposed emphasizer belonging to the noun phrase, covered in the determiner dictionary. Used as a pronoun in ordinary modern prose it reads as costume; use it only when the archaism is deliberate or the document is a contract that has always said it.
entries.see also: whatever, whichsoever, whomsoever, whosoever, whatsoever (determiner)

entries.meaning: 'Any one that' — picks a single member out of a set the sentence has already established.
examples: Take whichever you like — they're all the same price.
The warranty runs three years or 36,000 miles, whichever comes first.
Whichever of the two routes you pick, expect traffic.
She'll be happy with whichever they send.
Whichever is cheapest is the one we'll book.
We can meet Tuesday or Thursday, whichever works better for you.

senses.head: The one selected (fused relative)
body: We'll take whichever is cheapest. 2. No matter which (concessive). Whichever you pick, someone will complain.
examples: Take whichever you like — they're all the same price.
The warranty runs three years or 36,000 miles, whichever comes first.
Whichever of the two routes you pick, expect traffic.
She'll be happy with whichever they send.
Whichever is cheapest is the one we'll book.
We can meet Tuesday or Thursday, whichever works better for you.

entries.pronunciation note: accent on -ev-; conservative and Southern speakers have /hwɪtʃˈɛvɚ/
entries.русский: какой (который) угодно из; какой бы ни — выбор из известного ограниченного набора
entries.case: none — invariant
entries.register: neutral; standard in contracts and specifications
entries.type: fused relative pronoun, and concessive pronoun
entries.person / number: third person, invariant, singular for agreement.
entries.refers to: one member selected from a known, limited set — things, and people too when they are being selected from a set (whichever of the twins answers). Outside the who- forms, this is the one -ever pronoun that takes people comfortably, because the selection rather than the humanity is the point.
entries.agreement: singular verb — Whichever comes first is fine. It stays singular even over a plural of-phrase: Whichever of these routes is shortest works for me.
entries.pattern: whichever [verb] · whichever of [the/these/my + plural noun] · whichever of [them/us] · [verb] whichever [subject] [verb] · Whichever [clause], [main clause] — concessive · the fixed tie-breaker whichever comes first / is greater / is less
entries.contrast: against whatever, the difference is whether the range is closed. Take whatever you want opens the whole world; take whichever you want assumes a set already in view. That is why contracts say three years or 36,000 miles, whichever comes first and never ✗ whatever comes first. The of test separates pronoun from determiner exactly as it does elsewhere: whichever of the two is a pronoun, whichever route is a determiner and belongs to the determiner dictionary. Do not write it as two words: ✗ which ever comes first.
entries.see also: whatever, whoever, whichsoever, whichever (determiner), which

entries.meaning: 'Any one at all that' — the archaic emphatic of whichever.
examples: The buyer may select whichsoever of the parcels he prefers.
Whichsoever of the two conditions occurs first shall govern.
The court may impose a fine or imprisonment, whichsoever it deems appropriate.
He would take whichsoever of the roads was open to him that night.
Whichsoever is greater shall be paid within thirty days of demand.
They accepted whichsoever the arbitrator proposed.
entries.pronunciation note: main accent on -ev-, secondary on which-
entries.русский: какой бы то ни было из — устар., юр.; в современном языке практически не встречается
entries.case: none — invariant
entries.register: archaic and legal; effectively absent from ordinary modern English
entries.person / number: third person, invariant, singular for agreement.
entries.refers to: one member of a stated set, things or people, with the choice emphatically unrestricted.
entries.agreement: singular verb — Whichsoever is greater shall govern.
entries.pattern: whichsoever [verb] · whichsoever of [the + plural noun] · [verb] whichsoever [subject] [verb]
entries.contrast: the emphatic twin of whichever, with the same closed-set meaning and none of the currency. In a modern contract, whichever does the identical work and reads as English rather than as pastiche; keep whichsoever for quoting instruments that already contain it. Like every member of the -soever family it is one word: ✗ which so ever.
entries.see also: whichever, whatsoever, whosoever, whichsoever (determiner)

entries.meaning: 'Anyone who' — names a person by what they do rather than by who they are.
examples: Whoever parked in my spot is going to hear about it.
Give the extra ticket to whoever wants it.
Whoever is in charge here needs to fix the thermostat.
I'll go with whoever is driving.
Whoever you are, please stop calling this number.
The job goes to whoever applies first.
Whoever said that clearly hadn't read the report.

senses.head: Anyone who (fused relative)
body: Whoever finds it can keep it. 2. No matter who (concessive). Whoever she is, she has a lot of nerve. 3. The unidentified agent. With a mild note of exasperation or admiration: Whoever designed this parking garage should be prosecuted.
examples: Whoever parked in my spot is going to hear about it.
Give the extra ticket to whoever wants it.
Whoever is in charge here needs to fix the thermostat.
I'll go with whoever is driving.
Whoever you are, please stop calling this number.
The job goes to whoever applies first.
Whoever said that clearly hadn't read the report.

entries.pronunciation note: accent on -ev-; the w has been silent for centuries, so the word begins with a plain /h/. In rapid speech a linking glide appears between the vowels: [hʊˈwɛvɚ]
entries.русский: тот, кто; кто бы ни — только о людях; падеж берётся из своего придаточного
entries.case: subject — and the case is taken from the inner clause
entries.register: neutral; now the everyday form for both cases
entries.type: fused relative pronoun, and concessive pronoun
entries.person / number: third person; singular for verb agreement, though the follow-up pronoun is normally singular they, which is standard American English and needs no repair — Whoever left this should come get their coat.
entries.refers to: people only — "anyone who," "the person who." For things use whatever or whichever.
entries.agreement: singular verb inside the clause — Whoever wants seconds should say so, ✗ Whoever want. The outer verb is singular too, because the whole clause counts as one subject: Whoever ate the last donut owes me one.
entries.pattern: whoever [verb] — subject of its own clause · [preposition] whoever [verb] — to whoever answers · [verb] whoever [verb] · whoever [subject] is/are — as complement, whoever you are · Whoever [clause], [main clause] — concessive
entries.contrast: the case comes from the inner clause, not from what stands in front of it. In Give the file to whoever answers the phone, the preposition to governs the entire fused relative clause, not the pronoun; inside that clause whoever is the subject of answers, so the subject form is correct and ✗ to whomever answers the phone is a hypercorrection. The test: isolate the inner clause and substitute he or him — he answers the phone → whoever; you choose him → whomever. Honest note: in speech whoever is now used in both roles (Invite whoever you want) and nobody blinks; a conservative editor will still change that one to whomever in formal prose. Two words is a different thing again: Who ever told you that? is an intensified question.
entries.see also: whomever, whosever, whosoever, whatever, as many as, who, they (generic)

entries.meaning: 'Anyone whom' — names the person who is the object of the action in the inner clause.
examples: Send the invoice to whomever you dealt with at the agency.
She will support whomever the party nominates.
He was ready to argue with whomever he met that evening.
Award the contract to whomever the committee selects.
Whomever they choose, the transition is going to be rough.
Address the letter to whomever it concerns.
entries.pronunciation note: accent on -ev-; silent w, so it opens with /h/
entries.русский: того, кого; кому бы ни — объектная форма whoever; книжн., в речи редка
entries.case: object — taken from the inner clause
entries.register: formal; rare in speech, and when it does surface there it is more often wrong than right
entries.person / number: third person, people only, singular for agreement.
entries.refers to: people only, in the role of object of a verb or of a preposition inside its own clause.
entries.agreement: none of its own — it is an object, so the verb inside the clause agrees with that clause's own subject: whomever you choose, whomever the committee selects.
entries.pattern: [verb] whomever [subject] [verb] · [preposition] whomever [subject] [verb] · whomever [subject] [verb], [main clause] — fronted concessive · the fixed formula to whomever it may concern
entries.contrast: whomever is correct only where it is the object inside its own clause: Give it to whomever you choose (you choose him) against Give it to whoever answers (he answers). A preposition in front of the clause is irrelevant, and reacting to it is precisely what produces the classic error ✗ Give it to whomever answers the phone. The he/him test settles every case in a second. Where whomever is genuinely alive is right after a preposition, in the fixed formulas — to whomever it may concern, to whomever these presents shall come — which is exactly where plain whom survives too. Be honest about the state of the word: outside that one construction whomever has essentially left the language, whoever is standard in speech in both roles, and in writing a wrong whomever is far more conspicuous than a whoever a purist would have changed. If you cannot verify the object role, write whoever — or rewrite the sentence.
entries.see also: whoever, whomsoever, whom, who

entries.meaning: 'Anyone at all whom' — the archaic emphatic object form.
examples: The estate passes to whomsoever the testator names in the codicil.
He would defend whomsoever the court appointed him to defend.
Notice may be served upon whomsoever the company designates as its agent.
Whomsoever the king favored rose quickly at court.
The reward was offered to whomsoever the sheriff should name.
She spoke freely to whomsoever she trusted.
entries.pronunciation note: main accent on -ev-, secondary on whom-
entries.русский: кого бы то ни было — устар., юр. объектная форма whosoever
entries.case: object, from the inner clause
entries.register: archaic and legal
entries.person / number: third person, people only, singular for agreement.
entries.refers to: people only, as object of a verb or preposition inside its own clause.
entries.agreement: none of its own; the inner verb agrees with the inner subject.
entries.pattern: [verb] whomsoever [subject] [verb] · [preposition] whomsoever [subject] [verb] · to whomsoever these presents shall come (a fixed opening in deeds)
entries.contrast: the emphatic twin of whomever, and it carries exactly the same object-case requirement — which the legal writers who reach for it routinely get wrong, producing ✗ to whomsoever shall apply where the pronoun is the subject of shall apply and whosoever is the correct form. The he/him test applies unchanged. In anything that is not a quotation or a deed, use whoever or whomever.
entries.see also: whomever, whosoever, whatsoever, whom

entries.meaning: 'The one belonging to whoever' — a possessive that supplies its own antecedent.
examples: Whosever this coat is, it has been on that hook for a week.
The wallet goes back to whosever it turns out to be.
Whosever the mistake was, the client is the one who paid for it.
Whoever's this is, they left the lights on. (the ordinary spoken form)
He said he would take whoever's was left over.
Whosever the responsibility was, nobody has admitted to it yet.
entries.pronunciation note: accent on -ev-; silent w. The everyday spoken equivalent is whoever's /huˈɛvɚz/, and the legal whosesoever /ˌhuzəsoʊˈɛvɚ/ is vanishingly rare
entries.русский: тот, чей; чей бы ни — притяжательная форма; редк. и книжн.
entries.case: possessive, standing alone
entries.register: rare and formal; most Americans avoid the word entirely
entries.person / number: third person, people (occasionally an organization), invariant.
entries.refers to: the possessor — "the person whose," "anyone whose." Human possessors in practice; a nonhuman possessor is vanishingly rare with this -ever form and is better rewritten with of which. Do not carry that limitation over to plain relative whose, which covers both people and things and always has (a book whose cover was torn); the objection to it is a superstition, not a rule.
entries.agreement: singular verb — Whosever it is has left it here a week.
entries.pattern: Whosever [clause], [main clause] · [preposition] whosever [subject] [verb] · everyday spoken form: whoever's [verb]
entries.contrast: the pronoun whosever stands alone (Whosever this is, it needs a name on it); whosever immediately followed by a noun (whosever car is blocking the drive) is a determiner and lives in the determiner dictionary. Everyday American English sidesteps both: whoever's, or a rewrite as whoever owns this. Two spelling traps: ✗ whoevers without the apostrophe is simply an error, and ✗ who's is who is, never a possessive. The personal possessive pronouns are the family that never takes an apostrophe — its, hers, ours, theirs, yours, and whose/whosever with them. Do not over-apply that: the possessive of generic one and of the indefinites is written with an apostrophe — one's, somebody's, each other's — and the everyday whoever's belongs with those, since it is built with the genitive 's rather than being an inherited possessive form. What has no apostrophe is the fused word whosever itself.
entries.see also: whoever, whomever, whose, whosever (determiner)

entries.meaning: 'Anyone at all who' — the archaic emphatic of whoever. ---
examples: Whosoever believeth in him shall not perish.
Whosoever shall enter these gates does so at his own risk.
Whosoever holds this hammer, if he be worthy, shall possess the power of Thor.
Whosoever is found in violation shall forfeit the deposit.
Whosoever will may come.
The blessing extends to whosoever asks for it.
entries.pronunciation note: main accent on -ev-, secondary on who-; silent w
entries.русский: всякий, кто; кто бы то ни был — устар., библ., юр. усиленное whoever
entries.case: subject, from the inner clause
entries.register: archaic, biblical, and legal
entries.person / number: third person, people only, singular for agreement.
entries.refers to: people, with the range emphatically unrestricted — "anyone at all who."
entries.agreement: singular verb, and the older texts carry the archaic inflection to match: whosoever believeth, whosoever shall enter.
entries.pattern: Whosoever [verb], [main clause] · Whosoever [verb] shall [verb] · [preposition] whosoever [verb]
entries.contrast: the emphatic form of whoever, and the subject member of the pair with whomsoever — whosoever asks (he asks), whomsoever you ask (you ask him). It survives in scripture, hymn, statute, and deliberate archaism, and nowhere else; in modern prose whoever says the same thing without the costume. One word, always: ✗ who so ever.
entries.see also: whoever, whomsoever, whatsoever, whichsoever

entries.term: a person, a guy, a fella
entries.meaning: 'Anyone at all, and probably me' — a plain noun doing a pronoun's job.
examples: A person can only take so much of that.
It's the kind of job that wears a person out.
What's a person supposed to do with a bill like this?
A person's word ought to count for something. (the possessive, spelled with an apostrophe)
A guy could get used to living like this. (informal, and still male to many hearers)
A fella can't get a decent cup of coffee anywhere in this town. (folksy; older rural, Southern, and Midwestern speech, and dialect writing)
The formal equivalent is one can only take so much; the ordinary spoken one is you can only take so much.

senses.head: People in general
body: The generic proper: A person can only take so much. 2. The veiled first person. The speaker, at one remove and with a complaint attached: A person could starve around here. 3. The rhetorical question. What's a person supposed to do?

entries.pronunciation note: the article is the weak /ə/ and never /eɪ/ — a stressed A person is counting people, not being generic. a guy /ə ˈɡaɪ/ uh-GY; a fella /ə ˈfɛlə/ uh-FEL-uh, a worn-down fellow, also spelled feller /ˈfɛlɚ/ in dialect writing. The possessive adds /z/: a person's [ə ˈpɚsənz], a guy's [ə ˈɡaɪz]
entries.русский: человек; парень; разг. мужик — «любой на моём месте», часто о самом говорящем
entries.case: none — one form for subject and object; possessive a person's, a guy's, a fella's
entries.register: a person neutral and conversational; a guy informal; a fella informal and folksy, at home in older rural, Southern, and Midwestern speech and used in print to signal exactly that
entries.type: generic human noun phrase used as a pronoun — a quasi-pronoun, not a pronoun proper
entries.person / number: third person singular, with a singular verb. The follow-up pronoun in ordinary modern American English is singular they — A person can't help how they feel — which is standard and needs no repair.
entries.refers to: anybody at all in the situation described, with the speaker very often included, which is the whole point of the construction: A person could get killed out there is usually a complaint about the speaker's own morning.
entries.agreement: singular verb — a person gets tired, a guy has to eat somewhere. ✗ a person get tired. The possessive is written with an apostrophe (a person's own money), like every noun and unlike the personal possessive pronouns.
entries.pattern: a person [singular verb] · [verb or preposition] a person — it wears a person out, hard on a person · a person's [noun] · what's a person to do? · a guy can't [verb] · a fella [singular verb]
entries.contrast: these are nouns, and that is what separates them from every true generic in this file: they need an article, they take the 's possessive, and they can be modified (a reasonable person, a young guy). What they buy is warmth. Formal writing takes one, ordinary speech takes generic you, and a person is what a speaker reaches for when you would land as an accusation: A person could starve waiting for this kitchen blames nobody in the room. Two labels, stated plainly. A guy began as and for many hearers remains male, so it is not a safe all-purpose generic in writing — a guy can't win said of a woman's situation will strike a fair number of readers as off. A fella is regional and dated — older rural, Southern, and Midwestern speech, with the eye-dialect spelling feller — and in print it is a costume, worn on purpose. The archaic ancestor of the whole pattern is a body, two centuries older and preserved for everyone in one Burns song. Note the determiner split as well: the article a is a determiner and is entered in the determiner dictionary; what does the pronoun's work here is the whole phrase, not the article.
entries.variants: a fella and the eye-dialect a feller (both worn-down spellings of a fellow), a body (archaic and dialectal), a person's / a guy's (possessive)
entries.see also: one (generic), you (generic), they (generic), Joe Blow, Joe Schmo, John Q. Public, every Tom, Dick, and Harry, a body, somebody, you guys, a

entries.meaning: 'I, under oath' — the person swearing a statement, named in the third person by the statement itself.
examples: Deponent says that he is over the age of eighteen and competent to testify to the matters set out below.
Affiant further states that the signature on the second page is her own.
Further affiant sayeth naught. (the closing fossil; also written Further deponent saith not)
Deponent examined the payroll records himself before signing this statement. (third-person reflexive, because the grammar is third person)
The clerk would not accept the form because affiant had not initialed the correction on page three.
The modern federal version drops the device altogether: I declare under penalty of perjury that the foregoing is true and correct.
Put the article back and the pronoun is gone: the deponent was cross-examined for six hours. (somebody else describing him)

senses.head: The opening frame
body: Deponent says that he is the owner of the vehicle described above. 2. The closing formula. Further affiant sayeth naught — a fossil meaning "that is all I have to say," and the last line of countless affidavits. 3. With the article, and not this use. The deponent contradicted himself twice is somebody else talking about him.

entries.pronunciation note: accent on the second syllable, the first vowel reduced to /ɪ/ or /ə/ and the last to /ə/; ✗ DEE-po-nent is a spelling pronunciation. affiant /əˈfaɪənt/ uh-FY-unt has three syllables with the accent on the second and a weak /ənt/ at the end, not ✗ AF-fee-ant. Neither word has a weak form in the sentence: used bare it opens its clause and carries the accent. The frozen closing keeps the archaic sayeth /ˈseɪəθ/ SAY-uth and saith /sɛθ/ SETH
entries.русский: юр. заявитель, дающий показания под присягой — о себе самом в третьем лице
entries.case: none — one form for subject and object; possessive deponent's, affiant's
entries.register: legal only, and formulaic even there. An American meets it in an affidavit, a sworn declaration, a deposition transcript, or a notarized statement, and almost always in one of two frames — the opening Deponent says that… and the closing Further affiant sayeth naught
entries.type: legal noun used bare as an impersonal self-reference — a third-person noun standing in for I
entries.person / number: grammatically third person singular, with a singular verb and third-person concord, although what it denotes is the first person — the man or woman swearing the statement.
entries.refers to: the individual making the sworn statement, and nobody else. The pronominal use is the bare one, with no article: Deponent states… Put the article back and it is an ordinary noun phrase pointing at a party from outside — the deponent was cross-examined for six hours is what the other side's brief says about him.
entries.agreement: singular verb — Deponent states that…, Affiant is over the age of eighteen, Further deponent saith not. ✗ Deponent state. Because the grammar is third person, the reflexive is himself or herself and never ✗ myself: Deponent examined the records himself.
entries.pattern: Deponent [singular verb] that [clause] · Affiant [singular verb] · Affiant further states that [clause] · the closings Further affiant sayeth naught and Further deponent saith not · deponent's [noun] · with the article, and no longer pronominal: the deponent, the affiant
entries.contrast: the whole pronominal effect sits in the missing article. Deponent says is the writer referring to himself in the third person; the deponent says is somebody else referring to him. Between the two words: affiant is the American term and goes with affidavit — the person who swears a written statement — while deponent covers that and also the witness giving oral testimony at a deposition, and it is the older word and the commoner one in British and older American practice. Against the neighbors that do the same job in other rooms: the undersigned is the contract's version and means whoever signed it, the present writer is the scholar's, and yours truly is the joke. Say the modern practice plainly — federal court forms and the plain-language drafting movement write I: I am over eighteen and competent to testify to the matters stated below. Two traps. Sayeth and saith are frozen archaisms and take no half-modernizing: ✗ further affiant says naught is neither one thing nor the other. And deponent has an unrelated life in grammar books, where a deponent verb is a Latin or Greek verb passive in form and active in meaning — no connection to this word beyond the shared root.
entries.variants: affiant (the American affidavit term), declarant (the modern federal equivalent, in a declaration under penalty of perjury), the deponent and the affiant (with the article — ordinary noun phrases, not this use)
entries.see also: the present writer, the present author, yours truly, he (generic), one (generic), the undersigned, the aforesaid, the aforementioned, the premises, I

entries.meaning: 'Anybody at all, and far too many of them' — three men's names doing a pronoun's work, and doing it with contempt.
examples: Every Tom, Dick, and Harry has an opinion about the school board these days.
Once the gate code got out, every Tom, Dick, and Harry in the county was parking in that lot.
You can't hand the master key to any Tom, Dick, or Harry who fills out a form.
They are not going to hire just any Tom, Dick, or Harry for a job that needs a clearance.
He complains that the certification has been handed to every Tom, Dick, and Harry with four hundred dollars and a weekend free.
Note the verb: every Tom, Dick, and Harry has an opinion, never ✗ have — every keeps the phrase singular.
The neutral version is everybody has an opinion; this phrase is never the neutral one.

senses.head: The crowd complaint
body: The core use: something once restricted is now open to anyone, and the speaker minds. Every Tom, Dick, and Harry has a podcast now. 2. The licensing frame. Not just any Tom, Dick, or Harry — used to insist that a qualification is required after all. 3. Frozen, and not about anybody named Tom. The three names cannot be swapped for others and leave the idiom standing.

entries.pronunciation note: each of the three names carries a beat and the heaviest falls on Harry; the and is only ever weak — /ən/ or a syllabic /n̩/, never the full /ænd/ — which makes the phrase a syllable shorter than it looks on the page. every is two syllables in ordinary American speech, [ˈɛvri], not three. In any Tom, Dick, or Harry the or is the weak /ɚ/
entries.русский: всякий встречный-поперечный — люди без разбора; всегда пренебрежительно
entries.case: none — one form for subject and object; the possessive every Tom, Dick, and Harry's is grammatical and so ungainly that writers rewrite around it
entries.register: informal to neutral, and always disparaging. It says that the people in question are undistinguished and that there are far more of them than anybody wanted; there is no complimentary use of it and no neutral one
entries.type: fixed generic noun phrase used as a pronoun — a quasi-pronoun, not a pronoun proper
entries.person / number: third person singular for agreement, in spite of naming three people — every is a distributive singular and governs the whole phrase.
entries.refers to: people in general, taken indiscriminately — "anybody at all, and more of them than there ought to be." It never points at three particular men named Tom, Dick, and Harry, and it never points at one person.
entries.agreement: singular verb — Every Tom, Dick, and Harry has an opinion about it, ✗ Every Tom, Dick, and Harry have an opinion. That is the ordinary behavior of every, which stays singular however long the list behind it — compare every man, woman, and child was accounted for. The any variant is singular too: any Tom, Dick, or Harry who walks in off the street.
entries.pattern: every Tom, Dick, and Harry [singular verb] · [verb or preposition] every Tom, Dick, and Harry · any Tom, Dick, or Harry [relative clause] · the licensing frame not just any Tom, Dick, or Harry · the bare Tom, Dick, and Harry after all
entries.contrast: against the other placeholder names the difference is one against many. Joe Blow and John Q. Public name one ordinary person; every Tom, Dick, and Harry names the crowd, and the crowd is the complaint. Against neutral everybody: the meaning is the same and the attitude is not — everybody has an opinion reports, every Tom, Dick, and Harry has an opinion sneers. Against all and sundry, which is the formal-jocular version of the same idea and manages it without naming anybody. Two labels stated plainly. The names are male, all three of them, which puts the phrase in the position generic he is in — it asks men's names to stand for people in general, and there is no established feminine counterpart. And the Dick of it is now why a fair number of American speakers steer around the phrase in public, the vulgar sense of the word being unavoidable to a modern ear even though it plays no part in the idiom. The neutral rewrites are everybody, anybody at all, and all comers. Mechanics: the names keep their capitals, the commas are the ordinary commas of a list, and the serial comma before and is the commoner spelling, though house styles that drop the serial comma elsewhere drop it here too — every Tom, Dick and Harry is not an error.
entries.variants: any Tom, Dick, or Harry, the bare Tom, Dick, and Harry after all, and the spellings without the serial comma — every Tom, Dick and Harry, any Tom, Dick or Harry
entries.see also: Joe Blow, Joe Schmo, John Q. Public, a person, a guy, a fella, such and such, so-and-so, they (generic), everybody, anybody, all and sundry, one and all

entries.meaning: 'Anyone at all, referred to as though male' — the traditional generic, now replaced by singular they.
examples: If anyone calls, tell him I'll be back at two. (dated; now tell them)
He who hesitates is lost. (a frozen proverb, quoted rather than produced)
Every applicant is entitled to a hearing before he is dismissed. (dated; now before they are dismissed)
No employee may authorize a payment to himself. (the generic reflexive; the modern fix is the plural — employees … themselves)
One should do what he thinks best. (older American practice after generic one; now what one thinks best, or what they think best)
The reader may judge for himself whether the argument holds. (older essayistic style; now readers can judge for themselves)
A witness must answer unless he invokes the privilege. (older statutory drafting; modern drafting uses they)

senses.head: Generic with an indefinite antecedent
body: If anyone calls, tell him I'll be back. — dated; now tell them. 2. Generic after one. The older American practice: One should do what he thinks best. 3. Legal and archaic survivals. Statutes, deeds, and bylaws drafted before the 1980s, usually with an interpretation clause attached. 4. Frozen proverbs. He who hesitates is lost — quoted, not produced.

The object him is /hɪm/ with weak /ɪm/ (tell him [ˈtɛlɪm], get him [ˈɡɛɾɪm]), and her, in the paired he or she, is /hɚ/ with weak /ɚ/, so call her comes out like caller
entries.русский: он — обобщённо о человеке любого пола; устар., вне нормы совр. амер. прозы
entries.case: subject; object him; standalone possessive his; reflexive himself
entries.register: the prescribed formal choice into the 1970s; now read as dated and as excluding, and current mainly in older statutes, deeds, and bylaws
entries.type: generic (epicene) pronoun — dated, and no longer standard in American edited prose
entries.person / number: third person singular, masculine in form — and the whole difficulty is that the generic use asks a masculine form to stand for people of any gender.
entries.refers to: a person of unspecified or unknown sex — anyone who fits the description — normally licensed by a singular indefinite antecedent (anyone, a driver, each applicant). Pointing at one identified man is not this word at all but the ordinary personal pronoun he.
entries.agreement: singular verb — he is, he has, he does. ✗ he are. The generic use changes nothing about agreement; what it changes is who the sentence sounds like it is about.
entries.pattern: [singular indefinite] … he [singular verb] — If anyone calls, he can leave a message · [verb] him · [preposition] him · himself · the paired he or she / him or her · the drafting formula words importing the masculine include the feminine
entries.contrast: three replacements, in the order an American editor reaches for them. Singular they is the ordinary modern solution and is standard American English — If anyone calls, they can leave a message. The plural rewrite removes the problem instead of patching it: Applicants must list their previous employers. The paired he or she is grammatical and tolerable once, unreadable when repeated, and it leaves out people who are neither; see his or her. Be precise about what is wrong with generic he: it is not a grammatical error, and it is what American style guides prescribed for most of the twentieth century — the objection is a usage objection, supported by reading studies in which people picture a man, and the form is now out of step with edited American practice. In an old instrument, leave it and read it as that document's own interpretation clause directs. Against generic one: the older American pattern switched to he after the first one (One should do what he thinks best), which is this same dated construction in a different frame. Note also the split with the determiner: he and him are pronouns and belong here, while generic his in every applicant must bring his ID is a possessive determiner and is covered in the determiner dictionary.
entries.see also: one (generic), they (generic), you (generic), whoever, he, him, themself, his or her

entries.meaning: 'One person, sex unstated' — the paired form that replaced generic he and has itself been replaced by singular they.
examples: If a customer is unhappy with the order, he or she can return it within thirty days. (now ordinarily they can return it)
Each participant will be told privately how he or she scored on the pretest.
The applicant must sign the form himself or herself in the presence of a notary. (the paired reflexive)
She or he will be assigned a mentor for the first year. (reversed order, used for balance)
Ask the patient whether he or she has taken anything for the pain. (older clinical style; current guidance prefers they)
Any employee who witnesses an injury must report it to his or her supervisor. (the possessive determiner — a determiner, not a pronoun)
Each student must bring his or her laptop so that he or she can upload his or her work. (perfectly grammatical, and exactly why the form fell out of favor)

senses.head: With an indefinite antecedent
body: The core use: Each applicant should bring proof that he or she is a resident. 2. Legal and procedural drafting. Where a document sets out to name both sexes explicitly, often with an interpretation clause behind it. 3. Reversed for balance. She or he — used to keep the feminine form from always coming second, and no less correct.

The h of he survives here because the word carries a beat, unlike the weak /i/ of is he [ˈɪzi]. Written he/she is read aloud as this phrase, and s/he has no spoken form of its own at all

entries.case: subject; object him or her; possessive determiner his or her, standalone possessive his or hers; reflexive himself or herself
entries.register: formal and careful — the prescribed repair for generic he from roughly 1980 to 2010, still the house style in some legal and technical drafting, and now read as dated and bureaucratic beside singular they
entries.person / number: third person singular throughout — he or she is one person, not two, whatever the coordination looks like.
entries.refers to: a single person of unspecified or unknown sex, licensed by a singular indefinite or role-based antecedent (each applicant, anyone, the tenant). It cannot point at an identified person, and it names two sexes, so it does not cover people who are neither.
entries.agreement: singular verb — If a customer calls, he or she is entitled to a refund. ✗ he or she are. The reflexive is the paired himself or herself, and the possessive determiner is his or her, which must precede a noun and therefore belongs with the determiners.
entries.pattern: [singular indefinite antecedent] … he or she [singular verb] · the reversed she or he · written he/she, (s)he, s/he · object him or her · his or her [noun], his or hers standing alone · reflexive himself or herself · the drafting tag he or she, as the case may be
entries.contrast: grammatical, inclusive of two sexes, and unreadable in bulk — the objection is never to one use but to the fourth in a paragraph: Each student must bring his or her laptop so that he or she can upload his or her work. Three replacements, in the order an American editor reaches for them. Singular they is standard American English, entered in Merriam-Webster and accepted by AP and Chicago — If a customer calls, they are entitled to a refund. The plural rewrite is usually better than either — Customers are entitled to a refund. The paired form is what remains when a document must spell both out. Say the coverage limit plainly: he or she names two sexes and leaves out people who are neither, which is the second reason edited practice has moved on. Case works here as in every coordination — subject he or she, object him or her: ✗ Give it to he or she, ✗ between he or she and the landlord. And do not mix strategies inside one sentence: ✗ If anyone calls, take their number and tell him or her I'll ring back.
entries.variants: she or he, he/she, she/he, s/he, (s)he, and in older drafting he or she, as the case may be

entries.meaning: The object half of the paired generic — he or she after a verb or a preposition.
examples: If a client asks for the file, give it to him or her the same day. (now ordinarily give it to them)
Notify him or her in writing at least ten days before the hearing.
The award will be presented to him or her at the June meeting.
Ask him or her to initial the second page and return it.
Any dispute between the tenant and him or her goes to arbitration. (object of a preposition)
Whoever is on call should keep the pager with him or her overnight. (modern drafting: with them)
✗ Him or her should sign first → He or she should sign first. (the case error the pair invites)
entries.pronunciation note: all three words have weak forms and all three are used at once in running speech — him → /ɪm/, or → /ɚ/, her → /ɚ/ — so tell him or her comes out [ˈtɛl ɪm ɚ ˈhɚ] and, with the last word unaccented too, [ˈtɛl əm ɚ ɚ]. The h of her returns whenever the word carries the phrase accent. The reversed her or him is /ˌhɚ ɔr ˈhɪm/
entries.русский: его или её, ему или ей — объектная форма he or she; книжн., канцелярское
entries.case: object — the subject form is he or she; possessive determiner his or her, standalone possessive his or hers; reflexive himself or herself
entries.register: formal and careful, and dated in exactly the way its subject form is
entries.person / number: third person singular — one person, not two, and no verb agreement of its own.
entries.refers to: the same unspecified single person as he or she, standing after a verb or a preposition. Like the subject form it names two sexes and does not cover people who are neither.
entries.agreement: none of its own. It is an object, so the verb in the clause agrees with that clause's own subject: The clerk mails it to him or her, The clerks mail it to him or her.
entries.pattern: [verb] him or her · [preposition] him or her · give [something] to him or her · reversed her or him · written him/her · the drafting chain he or she … him or her … his or her
entries.contrast: case is the whole entry. Him or her is the object form and can never be a subject: ✗ Him or her should sign the form → He or she should sign it. The deletion test settles it as it settles every coordination — take one member out and read what is left: Give it to him ✓ and Give it to her ✓, so Give it to him or her ✓, while ✗ Him should sign exposes the subject error instantly. The same test kills the hypercorrection that goes the other way: ✗ between he or she and the landlord → between him or her and the landlord, because between is a preposition and takes the object form, exactly as in between you and me. On register, everything at he or she applies unchanged — singular them is the ordinary modern choice (Give it to them), and the plural rewrite is usually better than either. There is no written blend for this slot: him/her exists, ✗ s/him does not.
entries.see also: he or she, s/he, he (generic), him, them, his or her

entries.meaning: 'The same source, just above' — a footnote word that stands in for a citation instead of repeating it.
examples: Note 12 reads simply Ibid., 47 — the same book as note 11, at a different page.
A bare Ibid. with no page number means the same work and the same page as the note above it.
If note 8 cites two different books, note 9 cannot say Ibid. — there is nothing single for it to point at.
The copyeditor replaced every Ibid. in the chapter with a short-form citation, and the notes stopped being unreadable.
Insert one new note above a run of ibid. references and every one of them now cites the wrong book.
American legal writing does the same job with Id., which the Bluebook prescribes and which no brief goes three pages without.
Read aloud in a seminar, ibid. comes out as "same source" — nobody pronounces the Latin.

senses.head: Same work, same page
body: Bare Ibid. repeats the whole of the note above it. 2. Same work, new page. Ibid., 214 — the commonest form by a wide margin. 3. Where an American actually meets it. The notes of a humanities book, a Chicago-style paper, and older scholarship; a legal brief uses Id. instead, and a science paper uses neither, its citations being numbered.
examples: Note 12 reads simply Ibid., 47 — the same book as note 11, at a different page.
A bare Ibid. with no page number means the same work and the same page as the note above it.

Insert one new note above a run of ibid. references and every one of them now cites the wrong book.
