Read aloud in a seminar, ibid. comes out as "same source" — nobody pronounces the Latin.

entries.pronunciation note: two syllables, accent on the first, and the final d is fully released — the period on the page stops the spelling, not the word. The unabbreviated ibidem is /ɪˈbaɪdɛm/ or /ɪˈbɪdɛm/ ib-EYE-dem, accent on the second syllable, and is essentially never said aloud. There is no weak form: this is a written abbreviation, spoken only when somebody is reading a footnote out loud, and most Americans reading one out loud simply say same source
entries.русский: там же — в сноске: тот же источник (и та же страница), что в предыдущей ссылке
entries.case: none — invariant, and it never inflects
entries.register: scholarly and formal, and narrower now than it once was. An American meets it in the footnotes of a humanities book, in a Chicago-style notes-and-bibliography paper, and in older scholarship of every kind; the Chicago Manual of Style now prefers a shortened citation in its place, and American legal writing uses Id. and never ibid.
entries.type: scholarly citation pro-form — Latin ibidem, "in the same place," standing in the slot a citation would fill
entries.person / number: third person, with no number of its own — it inherits whatever the preceding citation had, one work or one volume out of many.
entries.refers to: the source cited immediately before it, and nothing else. It is strictly anaphoric and strictly adjacent: the note above it must name exactly one work, or ibid. has nothing to point at. Standing bare it means the same work and the same page; with a number after it, the same work at a new page.
entries.agreement: none — it governs no verb and enters into no concord. It is a pro-form for a noun phrase, not a subject.
entries.pattern: Ibid. — same work, same page · Ibid., [page number] — same work, new page · capitalized at the head of a note, lowercase inside a running sentence · the Bluebook equivalent Id. and Id. at [page] · the abandoned neighbors op. cit. and loc. cit.
entries.contrast: three Latin shorteners, pointing in three different directions. Ibid. points at the work just cited — same source, immediately above. Idem points at the author just cited, with a different work about to follow. Op. cit. points at a work cited somewhere earlier, not necessarily just above, which is exactly why it failed: the reader has to go hunting, and Chicago has dropped it. Against q.v., which points sideways — at another entry in the book you are holding — rather than backward at a source. Two rules produce most of the errors. Ibid. cannot follow a note that cited two or more works, because there is then no single antecedent for it. And it does not survive editing: insert one note above a run of them and every one now cites the wrong book, which is the practical reason copyeditors replace them with short-form citations. Mechanics: the period is part of the abbreviation and is not optional (✗ Ibid bare), current Chicago sets the word in roman rather than italic, and the capital belongs only where a note begins.
entries.variants: ibidem (the unabbreviated Latin), Id. (the American legal equivalent), and the abandoned op. cit. and loc. cit.
entries.see also: idem, q.v. (quod vide) / which see, the present writer, the present author, the aforesaid, the aforementioned, the foregoing, the same, the same

entries.meaning: 'The same one, just above' — a footnote word standing in for an author's name, or, in a brief, for the whole citation before it.
examples: The bibliography gives the first title in full and the second as Idem, The Later Essays, 1994.
Idem points at the author and ibid. at the work — that one line settles most of the confusion.
Every other citation in the brief is Id. at 412, which is how American legal writing avoids repeating a case name.
Chicago now advises writing the author's name out again rather than reaching for idem.
Idem is a Latin word and takes no period; ✗ idem. is an error no spell-checker will flag.
A note that reads Id. with nothing after it means the same source and the same page as the note above.
Older scholarship wrote eadem for a woman author, and current practice uses idem for everybody.

senses.head: Same author, new work
body: The humanities use: Idem, The Later Essays follows a note that has already named the author. 2. The abbreviation in a brief. Id. means the same authority, and the same page unless a page follows — the commonest word in a brief's citations. 3. Not an abbreviation. Idem is a whole Latin word and takes no period; id. is the abbreviation and takes one.
examples: The bibliography gives the first title in full and the second as Idem, The Later Essays, 1994.
Idem points at the author and ibid. at the work — that one line settles most of the confusion.
Every other citation in the brief is Id. at 412, which is how American legal writing avoids repeating a case name.
Chicago now advises writing the author's name out again rather than reaching for idem.
Idem is a Latin word and takes no period; ✗ idem. is an error no spell-checker will flag.
A note that reads Id. with nothing after it means the same source and the same page as the note above.
Older scholarship wrote eadem for a woman author, and current practice uses idem for everybody.

entries.pronunciation note: accent on the first syllable, both vowels full, no weak form. The abbreviation id. is /ɪd/ ID, one syllable, and in American legal writing it is far commoner than the full word — a lawyer reading a citation aloud says the two letters, or simply same
entries.русский: он же, тот же автор — в библиографии; в амер. юр. сокр. Id. — «там же»
entries.case: none — invariant in English use. Latin inflected it (eadem feminine, eidem plural) and English scholarship abandoned the inflection, so ✗ eadem for a woman author now reads as an affectation rather than as precision
entries.register: scholarly in its full form and legal in its abbreviation. An American meets idem spelled out in humanities bibliographies and older footnotes, and meets Id. in every American brief, memo, and judicial opinion, where the Bluebook makes it the standard short form
entries.type: scholarly and legal citation pro-form — Latin idem, "the same," standing in the slot an author's name would fill
entries.person / number: third person, with no number of its own — it inherits whatever it points back at.
entries.refers to: the same author as the citation immediately before, in humanities practice, with a different work about to be named. In American legal practice the abbreviation Id. refers instead to the whole preceding authority — the source, and the same page unless a new one is given.
entries.agreement: none — it governs no verb.
entries.pattern: Idem, [title], [publication details] — same author, new work · Id. — same authority, same page · Id. at [page] — same authority, new page · capitalized at the head of a note, lowercase inside a running sentence
entries.contrast: this is the entry where two traditions use one Latin word for two different jobs, and the difference is worth stating flatly. In humanities citation idem means the same author, and something new follows it: Idem, The Later Essays, 1994. In American legal citation Id. means the same authority altogether — which is the job ibid. does in Chicago style. So a lawyer's Id. and a historian's ibid. are equivalents, while a historian's idem is a different word doing a different thing, and reading a brief with the humanities sense in mind will mislead you on every page. Against ibid. directly, the split is work against author. Chicago now discourages idem on the plain ground that writing the author's name again costs three words and confuses nobody. Mechanics: idem is a complete Latin word and takes no period (✗ idem.), while id. is an abbreviation and must have one (✗ id bare); neither is italicized in current Chicago style, though older scholarship italicized both.
entries.variants: id. (the American legal abbreviation), eadem and ead. (the Latin feminine, now rare and generally avoided), the same (the plain English equivalent)
entries.see also: ibid., q.v. (quod vide) / which see, the present writer, the present author, the aforesaid, the aforementioned, the same, the same

entries.term: Joe Blow, Joe Schmo, John Q. Public
entries.meaning: 'The ordinary person, given a name' — a proper name pressed into service as a generic.
examples: The average Joe has no idea what any of this costs until the bill shows up.
Some Joe Blow off the street can walk in, sign one form, and take the whole file with him.
The rule was written for lawyers, not for John Q. Public.
Try explaining a deductible to your average Joe and see how far you get. (the informal ethical your)
He talks as though every customer were Joe Schmo who has never seen a contract before.
The average Joe's paycheck has not moved in real terms in twenty years. (the possessive)
Keep it apart from John Doe, which names one particular person nobody can identify — a placeholder for an identity, not a generic.

senses.head: The ordinary person
body: The core use: the average Joe has no idea what a deductible is. 2. Anybody at all, dismissively. Some Joe Blow off the street can walk in and sign for it. 3. The citizen. John Q. Public in journalism and civics — the public as the institution addresses it. 4. Not the unknown-identity placeholder. John Doe is one particular person without a name; Joe Blow is nobody in particular.
examples: The average Joe has no idea what any of this costs until the bill shows up.
Some Joe Blow off the street can walk in, sign one form, and take the whole file with him.
The rule was written for lawyers, not for John Q. Public.
Try explaining a deductible to your average Joe and see how far you get. (the informal ethical your)
He talks as though every customer were Joe Schmo who has never seen a contract before.
The average Joe's paycheck has not moved in real terms in twenty years. (the possessive)
Keep it apart from John Doe, which names one particular person nobody can identify — a placeholder for an identity, not a generic.

entries.pronunciation note: both words carry a beat and the heavier one falls on Blow. Joe Schmo /ˌdʒoʊ ˈʃmoʊ/ joe-SHMOH, spelled Schmoe and Shmoe as well, with the Yiddish shm- onset that no native English word has. John Q. Public /ˌdʒɑn kju ˈpʌblɪk/ john-cue-PUB-lik — the middle initial is said as the letter and is never expanded into a name. the average Joe /ði ˌævrɪdʒ ˈdʒoʊ/ thee-AV-rij-JOH, with the in its pre-vowel weak form /ði/ and average ordinarily two syllables, [ˈævrɪdʒ]. None of the names reduces: a placeholder name still has to be heard as a name
entries.русский: разг. рядовой обыватель, простой смертный — человек из толпы; все формы муж. рода
entries.case: none — one form for subject and object; possessive Joe Blow's, John Q. Public's, the average Joe's
entries.register: informal throughout, and each member carries its own attitude. The average Joe is the mildest and the only one an American is likely to write in ordinary prose; Joe Blow is dismissive; Joe Schmo is the most dismissive of the set, its shm- being the pattern English borrowed from Yiddish for making a word contemptible; John Q. Public is civic and journalistic — the ordinary citizen as the government or the press addresses him — and now reads as mid-century
entries.type: placeholder proper name used as a generic — a quasi-pronoun, not a pronoun proper
entries.person / number: third person singular, with a singular verb. The average Joe behaves like the ordinary noun phrase it is and pluralizes freely (average Joes); the bare names do not (✗ Joe Blows).
entries.refers to: the ordinary, unremarkable person — people in general, seen as one representative specimen. It is not a stand-in for a particular person whose name happens to be unknown, which is a different job done by a different set of names. All four forms are male.
entries.agreement: singular verb — Joe Blow doesn't read the fine print, The average Joe has no idea what any of that costs. ✗ The average Joe have. The follow-up pronoun is he, and because these are men's names singular they does not repair them the way it repairs generic he — the fix is to rewrite with the average person or most people.
entries.pattern: Joe Blow [singular verb] · some Joe Blow / any Joe Blow off the street · John Q. Public [singular verb] · the average Joe [singular verb] · your average Joe — with the informal ethical your · possessive the average Joe's [noun]
entries.contrast: three kinds of placeholder name, and only one of them is a generic. The generic — Joe Blow, Joe Schmo, John Q. Public, the average Joe — stands for people in general, and is what this entry covers. The unknown-identity placeholder — John Doe, Jane Doe, Richard Roe — stands for one particular person whose name the court or the hospital does not have; it is a name sitting in a name's slot, not a generic, and this file says so already at such and such, so-and-so. The forgotten name — what's-his-name, what's-her-name — stands for a person the speaker knows and cannot retrieve. Against a person, a guy, a fella: identical work done with a common noun instead of a name, which is exactly what leaves a person usable of anybody while Joe Blow is not. Against every Tom, Dick, and Harry: one ordinary person against a crowd of them. Label the gender plainly — all four are male in form, Jane Q. Public exists and is rare, and there is no established female counterpart in general use, so none of these is a safe all-purpose generic in writing; the neutral rewrites are the average person, the ordinary reader, most people, and the general public. Mechanics: the names keep their capitals, the average Joe keeps the capital on Joe alone, and ✗ the average joe is an error no spell-checker will catch.
entries.variants: the average Joe, your average Joe, Joe Schmoe and Joe Shmoe (spellings), Joe Sixpack (political and disparaging), Jane Q. Public, the man on the street, the average American, and the British Joe Bloggs and Fred Bloggs
entries.see also: a person, a guy, a fella, every Tom, Dick, and Harry, such and such, so-and-so, they (generic), you (generic), so-and-so, what's-his-name, what's-her-name, what's-his-face

entries.meaning: 'People in general, myself included' — states something as true of anybody in the situation.
examples: One cannot be too careful with contracts like this.
One does what one can.
It is the kind of book one reads twice.
One never knows how these things will turn out.
If one is going to complain, one should at least read the policy first.
The rules make it hard for one to plan more than a year ahead.
One should keep one's receipts until the warranty expires.

senses.head: People in general
body: The core use, and the formal counterpart of generic you: One cannot be too careful. 2. I, at a polite distance. In the mouth of a public figure, one is a modest disguise for I (One does what one can), which is exactly why it can sound arch.
examples: One cannot be too careful with contracts like this.
One does what one can.
It is the kind of book one reads twice.
One never knows how these things will turn out.
If one is going to complain, one should at least read the policy first.
The rules make it hard for one to plan more than a year ahead.
One should keep one's receipts until the warranty expires.

entries.pronunciation note: no weak form — generic one keeps at least a secondary accent, which is part of why it sounds formal. Homophone of won
entries.русский: обобщённое «человек», безличный оборот — книжн.; в амер. англ. звучит чопорно
entries.case: one form for subject and object; possessive one's; reflexive oneself
entries.register: formal, and in American English easily too formal — it can read as stuffy or affected
entries.person / number: grammatically third person singular; semantically it takes in the speaker and the hearer both — "people in general, myself among them."
entries.refers to: people in general, never a particular individual, and it can never take an antecedent: ✗ Maria said one was tired. It is also not a substitute for a noun already mentioned — that is the prop-word one (the red one), a different word.
entries.agreement: singular verb — one is, one has, one does, one doesn't. ✗ one are, ✗ one have.
entries.pattern: one [singular verb] · [verb] one · [preposition] one · one's [noun] · oneself · the fixed frames one would think, one never knows, if one may say so
entries.contrast: the transatlantic split is in the follow-up pronoun. Traditional American practice switched to he/his/himself after the first one — One should do what he thinks best — and that is what older American style guides prescribe; it now reads as both dated and pointedly gendered (see he (generic)). British practice repeats one (One should do what one thinks best), and current American editing has largely moved to that pattern or has dodged the construction altogether. What you must not do is mix the two inside a passage, or slide from one to you (✗ One should read the fine print before you sign). Against generic you: same meaning, opposite register — you is what Americans say, one is what they write when the tone is elevated. Generic one is also distinct from the prop-word one (the ones on the left) and from the numeral one, neither of which is generic.
entries.see also: oneself (generic), you (generic), they (generic), we (generic), he (generic), one, one's

entries.meaning: The reflexive that goes with generic one — the generic person acting on the generic person.
examples: One should not take oneself too seriously.
It is difficult to explain oneself under that kind of pressure.
There is a real satisfaction in doing it oneself.
One can easily talk oneself out of a perfectly good idea.
Living by oneself takes some getting used to.
One finds oneself agreeing with him against one's better judgment.
entries.pronunciation note: accent on -self; unstressed the first syllable reduces toward [wən]
entries.русский: себя, себе — возвратная форма обобщённого one; книжн.
entries.case: reflexive
entries.register: formal
entries.person / number: third person singular, invariant, gender-neutral. There is no plural: ✗ oneselves.
entries.refers to: generic one, in the same clause. It requires that antecedent — a named person cannot have it (✗ Maria hurt oneself).
entries.agreement: no verb agreement of its own; the verb agrees with one, which is singular.
entries.pattern: one [verb] oneself · [preposition] oneself · by oneself · to find oneself [verb-ing] · for oneself
entries.contrast: oneself is to generic one what yourself is to generic you and themselves to generic they. Older American prose writes himself after generic one (see he (generic)); British and current American prose write oneself, and oneself is now the safer choice, since the generic masculine reads as excluding. Nonstandard neighbors, labeled: the vernacular reflexives hisself and theirselves are nonstandard — general in Southern, Appalachian, and rural white vernaculars and in African American English, and more regular than the standard himself and themselves they replace — and they are entered at hisself and theirselves; there is no vernacular counterpart to oneself, because one is a written-register word to begin with. Mind the spelling split: oneself is the pronoun (one should not take oneself too seriously), while one's self is an ordinary noun phrase about identity (a lifetime spent constructing one's self). And like every reflexive, it needs its antecedent in the same clause — ✗ One hoped that the committee would approve oneself.
entries.see also: one (generic), you (generic), he (generic), oneself, one's

entries.meaning: 'He or she,' squeezed into one written form — a subject-only spelling that never learned how to be said aloud.
examples: If the applicant is under eighteen, s/he must have a parent or guardian co-sign the form.
The tenant must give thirty days' notice before s/he vacates the unit. (1980s drafting; current drafting says before they vacate)
Each participant is asked at intake what s/he hopes to get out of the program.
The staff handbook uses (s)he throughout, which quietly leaves he standing under the parentheses.
The old clause read "he/she shall notify the department in writing"; the revision reads "they shall notify the department in writing."
Read aloud at orientation, s/he comes out as he or she every time — which is the argument for writing it that way to begin with.
entries.pronunciation note: a spelling rather than a word: it has no pronunciation of its own, and a reader who meets it aloud says he or she, she or he, or — reading around it — they. There is no weak form because there is nothing of its own to reduce; the or in whatever the reader substitutes is the usual weak /ɚ/
entries.русский: он/она — письменный гибрид she и he; только подлежащее, канцелярско-анкетное
entries.case: subject only. No object or possessive form is built the same way: ✗ s/him, ✗ s/his. A writer who opens with s/he has to finish with him or her and his or her, and that asymmetry is one reason the form never settled
entries.register: written only, and institutional — intake forms, HR and school policies, social-work and education prose, and textbooks of the 1970s through the 1990s. Never spoken, and now largely displaced by singular they
entries.type: written epicene pronoun — an orthographic blend of she and he
entries.person / number: third person singular, with a singular verb.
entries.refers to: a single person of unspecified sex, with an indefinite or role-based antecedent (the applicant, the client, each student). Like he or she it names two sexes and does not cover people who are neither.
entries.agreement: singular verb — If the client cancels, s/he forfeits the deposit. ✗ s/he are.
entries.pattern: s/he [singular verb] · the variants (s)he and he/she in the same slot · object him/her, possessive his/her · the standard frame: [role noun] … s/he [modal] [verb]
entries.contrast: three written shortcuts that differ only in typography. S/he puts she first and can be read either way. (s)he treats the s as optional and so leaves he standing underneath, which is precisely the complaint against it. He/she spells both out and is the least ambiguous and the least readable. All three are subject-only, all three stop a reader who tries to say them, and the Chicago Manual of Style and most American editors advise against every one. The live replacements are the ones listed at he (generic): singular they, which is standard American English; the plural rewrite, usually the best of the three; and the spelled-out he or she where a document must name both sexes. Do not mix the shortcuts with anything else in a passage: ✗ If a student misses the deadline, s/he must email their advisor. And do not confuse the slash of s/he with the slash of and/or — this one joins two spellings of one word, not two options.
entries.variants: (s)he, he/she, she/he, with the object him/her and the possessive his/her
entries.see also: he or she, him or her, he (generic), they (generic), themself, his or her

entries.meaning: A deliberate blank — the speaker names the slot instead of the value, for a thing (such and such) or for a person (so-and-so).
examples: They tell you to fill out the form, do such and such, and call back in a week.
If you do such and such on the site, the system flags the account automatically.
Talk to so-and-so in payroll — she's the one who actually fixes these.
He's forever dropping names: lunch with so-and-so, golf with so-and-so's brother. (the possessive)
The old so-and-so still hasn't paid me back. (the mild insult, standing in for a stronger word)
Every one of those letters opens "Dear Mr. So-and-so" and then asks for money.
Put a noun behind it and it stops being a pronoun: such-and-such a date, such-and-such an amount are determiners.

senses.head: The worked example
body: Walking somebody through a procedure whose actual values do not matter yet: You do such and such, and if it fails they do such and such. 2. The unnamed person. Call so-and-so in accounting — the name exists and is beside the point. 3. The name withheld. The speaker knows it and will not say it. 4. The mild insult. The old so-and-so never paid me back — a euphemism standing in for a stronger word.
examples: They tell you to fill out the form, do such and such, and call back in a week.
If you do such and such on the site, the system flags the account automatically.
Talk to so-and-so in payroll — she's the one who actually fixes these.
He's forever dropping names: lunch with so-and-so, golf with so-and-so's brother. (the possessive)
The old so-and-so still hasn't paid me back. (the mild insult, standing in for a stronger word)
Every one of those letters opens "Dear Mr. So-and-so" and then asks for money.
Put a noun behind it and it stops being a pronoun: such-and-such a date, such-and-such an amount are determiners.

entries.pronunciation note: the and is only ever weak — /ən/ or a syllabic /n̩/, never the full /ænd/ — which is why the phrase is shorter than it looks on the page. so-and-so is /ˈsoʊ ən ˌsoʊ/ SOH-un-soh, accent on the first so, with the same weak and; the possessive so-and-so's adds /z/, and the insult plural so-and-sos takes /z/ too
entries.русский: то-то и то-то, такой-то — намеренная замена имени или значения; so-and-so — о человеке
entries.case: none — one form for subject and object; possessive so-and-so's
entries.register: neutral in speech and in explanatory writing; so-and-so for an unnamed person is informal, and so-and-so as a mild insult (the old so-and-so) is informal, euphemistic, and dated — an American now meets that sense mostly from older speakers and in mid-century writing
entries.type: placeholder pronouns — stand-ins for a name or a value the speaker declines to supply
entries.person / number: third person singular. So-and-so is the only one with a plural, and only in the insult sense: those so-and-sos.
entries.refers to: nothing in particular, on purpose. Such and such holds the place of a thing, a value, a date, or an action — "whatever it turns out to be." So-and-so holds the place of a person: one whose name is beside the point of the example, or one the speaker will not name.
entries.agreement: singular verb — So-and-so calls, and you take a message, Such and such happens, and the claim is denied. ✗ So-and-so call.
entries.pattern: do such and such · if you [verb] such and such, then [clause] · talk to so-and-so in [department] · Mr./Ms. So-and-so · so-and-so's [noun] · the insult frames the old so-and-so, you little so-and-so
entries.contrast: the slot test separates the pronoun from the determiner here exactly as it does everywhere else in these two dictionaries. Standing alone it is a pronoun — he claimed he had done such and such; in front of a noun it is a determiner and belongs to such-and-such (a) — such-and-such a date, such-and-such an amount. Against the neighbors: what's-his-name and what's-her-name stand in for a name the speaker has genuinely forgotten, where so-and-so stands in for one that was never worth supplying; thingamajig and whatchamacallit fill in an object's name; whatnot and and such close a list rather than filling a slot; and the legal placeholders John Doe and Jane Roe are proper names, not pronouns — as against the generic placeholder names Joe Blow, Joe Schmo, and John Q. Public, which do stand for people in general. Against demonstrative such: Such was the outcome points back at something real, while such and such points at a blank nobody has filled. Spelling: so-and-so is always hyphenated, and such and such is written open or hyphenated (such-and-such), neither being an error.
entries.variants: such-and-such (hyphenated spelling), thus and so (dated), so and so (rare open spelling)
entries.see also: such, such (demonstrative), whatnot, something or other, they (generic), Joe Blow, Joe Schmo, John Q. Public, such-and-such (a)

entries.term: the present writer, the present author
entries.meaning: 'I, at arm's length' — the writer of the page referring to himself or herself in the third person.
examples: The present writer has argued elsewhere that the statute was misread from the start.
In the present writer's view, the second experiment settles the question. (the possessive)
It seemed to the present author that nobody had gone back to the original source.
The author of the memoir was thirty when he wrote it; the present writer was not yet born. (the disambiguating use)
The present reviewer confesses to having enjoyed the first hundred pages and no more.
The modern version is simply I: I have argued elsewhere that the statute was misread. (accepted by APA, Chicago, and most journals)
The impersonal alternative drops the person altogether: it has been argued elsewhere that the statute was misread.

senses.head: Scholarly self-reference
body: The present writer has argued elsewhere that… 2. Disambiguation. In a paper about somebody else's book, the author means that book's author and the present writer means you — which is the one job the phrase still does well. 3. Modesty and its opposite. The device read as humble in 1930 and reads as pompous now.
examples: The present writer has argued elsewhere that the statute was misread from the start.
In the present writer's view, the second experiment settles the question. (the possessive)
It seemed to the present author that nobody had gone back to the original source.
The author of the memoir was thirty when he wrote it; the present writer was not yet born. (the disambiguating use)

entries.pronunciation note: the takes its weak /ðə/ before the consonant of present and its other weak form /ði/ before the vowel of author, so the present author is [ði ˈprɛzənt ˈɔθɚ]; present here is the adjective, accented on the first syllable /ˈprɛzənt/, never the verb /prɪˈzɛnt/
entries.русский: автор этих строк, пишущий эти строки — книжн., устар. вместо «я»
entries.case: none — one form for subject and object; possessive the present writer's
entries.register: formal, academic, and dated. An American meets it in older scholarly prose, book reviews, and mid-twentieth-century legal and scientific writing; in new writing it reads as arch or as false modesty, and plain I is now accepted by APA, Chicago, and most journals
entries.type: impersonal self-reference — a third-person noun phrase standing in for I
entries.person / number: grammatically third person singular — singular verb, third-person follow-up pronouns — although it denotes the first person, the one doing the writing.
entries.refers to: the author of the text in your hands, and nobody else. The word present is carrying the load: it separates the writer of this page from "the author" being discussed on it.
entries.agreement: singular verb — The present writer has argued elsewhere that… ✗ The present writer have. Keep the follow-up pronouns in the third person as well; sliding back into the first breaks the device: ✗ The present writer, in my view, would go further.
entries.pattern: the present writer [singular verb] · in the present writer's view / opinion / experience · it seems to the present writer that [clause] · the parallel forms the present author, the present reviewer, this writer, the undersigned (legal), your correspondent (journalism)
entries.contrast: four ways to keep I off the page, and they are not equals. The present writer is the stiffest, and it puts the writer into the third person outright. Editorial we (generic) is one writer wearing a plural pronoun (we show in Section 3) and is still ordinary in scientific papers. Generic one is a polite distance rather than a disguise, and in the mouth of a public figure it stands in for I (one does what one can). The passive and the impersonal it remove the person altogether (it is argued here that…) — the formal solution and the classic evasion in the same construction. Against plain I: American academic style has come around to it, APA recommends it outright, and the present writer now signals age rather than modesty. Three neighbors do adjacent jobs: the undersigned is legal boilerplate and means the person who signed, bare deponent and affiant do the same office at the head of an affidavit, and jocular yours truly means me with a wink. And do not switch frames inside a passage: pick I, or the editorial we, or the passive, and stay with it.
entries.variants: the present author, the present reviewer, this writer, this reviewer, the undersigned (legal), your correspondent (journalism)
entries.see also: we (generic), one (generic), oneself (generic), deponent, affiant, yours truly, it (extraposition), I, yours

entries.meaning: 'People — unspecified, unnameable, and not present' — attributes an action or a claim to nobody in particular.
examples: They say it's supposed to rain all weekend.
They're tearing down the old post office.
They don't make them the way they used to.
You can't fight city hall — they always win.
They raised the speed limit on that stretch last year.
In France they eat dinner much later than we do.
Apparently they found a cure for it years ago.

senses.head: Hearsay
body: They say… introduces something everybody has heard and nobody sourced. 2. The authorities. Whoever it is that makes the decisions: They're closing the exit ramp. 3. People in a place or trade. In France they eat much later.
examples: They say it's supposed to rain all weekend.
They're tearing down the old post office.
They don't make them the way they used to.
You can't fight city hall — they always win.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /ðe/ before a stressed verb, so they say runs to [ðe ˈseɪ] and they're to [ðɚ]. The object them has the weak form /ðəm/ → /əm/ — make them [ˈmeɪk əm], written 'em — and that reduction is ordinary General American, carrying no dialect marking whatever
entries.русский: они — неназванные «люди вообще»; по-русски обычно безлично: «говорят», «пишут»
entries.case: subject; object them; possessive determiner their, which is a determiner and is entered in the determiner dictionary; standalone possessive theirs
entries.register: informal to neutral; the formal alternative is the passive
entries.person / number: third person plural in form and in agreement, even though the group it names is entirely unspecified.
entries.refers to: nobody in particular — an unnamed, unidentifiable group: the people who know, the people in charge, people generally. Its defining property is that it has no antecedent and cannot be given one. If you can say who they are, it is not this pronoun.
entries.agreement: plural verb, always — they say, they're building, they've decided. ✗ they says.
entries.pattern: they say (that) [clause] · they [plural verb] · they're [verb-ing] · formal equivalents: it is said that, reportedly, the city says
entries.nonstandard: them standing in front of a noun — them apples, them boys — is not this pronoun and not a pronoun at all; it is a nonstandard demonstrative determiner, widespread in rural, Southern, Appalachian, and working-class American speech, and the standard form is those. Its entry is in the determiner dictionary; the weak /əm/ of I saw 'em is a separate matter and is standard everywhere. Nonstandard too, and in the other direction: ✗ they was and ✗ they says are the vernacular levelings of be and of the present tense — general in African American English and in Southern, Appalachian, and working-class white American speech, rule-governed there, and nonstandard in edited American English.
entries.contrast: keep three theys apart. Generic they has no antecedent (They say it's going to rain). Singular they does have one and is standard modern American English, including in edited prose (Someone left their coat) — it is entered in Merriam-Webster, accepted by the AP Stylebook and the Chicago Manual of Style, and attested since the fourteenth century, so say it plainly: it is not an error. Ordinary plural they points at a group already named. The ambiguity between the first and third is real: in They raised the rates again, they may be the utility company or nobody at all. In formal writing, replace generic they with the passive or with a named agent: They say the bridge will close → The bridge is reported to close / The city says the bridge will close. Notice too that an unnamed they is a rhetorical move — it asserts a source without supplying one.
entries.see also: we (generic), you (generic), one (generic), he (generic), it (extraposition), they, them

entries.meaning: 'People in general, and I am one of them' — states something as true of a group the speaker belongs to.
examples: We live in an age when nobody reads past the headline.
In this paper we argue that the second model fits the data better.
We don't say it that way in English.
How are we feeling this morning?
We have made our decision, and it is final.
We as a country have never really settled that question.
The results surprised us as much as they surprised anyone.

senses.head: Inclusive generic
body: We live in an age when nobody reads past the headline. 2. Editorial or authorial. One writer, plural pronoun: We argue in this paper that… 3. Royal. A monarch speaking as the institution. 4. Institutional. How are we feeling today? — meaning you.
examples: We live in an age when nobody reads past the headline.
In this paper we argue that the second model fits the data better.
We don't say it that way in English.
How are we feeling this morning?
We have made our decision, and it is final.
We as a country have never really settled that question.
The results surprised us as much as they surprised anyone.

entries.pronunciation note: unstressed it shortens toward [wɪ]; we're /wɪr/ reduces to [wɚ] and we've to [wɪv]. The object us has the weak form /əs/ — tell us [ˈtɛləs] — worn all the way down in let's
entries.русский: мы — обобщённо: люди, американцы, наша профессия; говорящий включён
entries.case: subject; object us; possessive determiner our, which is a determiner and is entered in the determiner dictionary; standalone possessive ours
entries.register: neutral; the editorial and royal uses are formal, and the institutional we is condescending
entries.person / number: first person plural in form and agreement — even when a single writer or a single monarch is meant.
entries.refers to: people in general with the speaker included and the hearer normally claimed as well — "humanity," "Americans," "this profession," "this journal," depending on context. English does not mark the inclusive/exclusive difference, so We're going to lunch may or may not be an invitation.
entries.agreement: plural verb, always — we are, we have, we were. ✗ we is, ✗ we was (nonstandard — the vernacular leveling of past be, general in African American English and in Southern, Appalachian, and working-class white American speech). Editorial we standing for one author still takes the plural: we show in Section 3 that…
entries.pattern: we [plural verb] · we all / we as a society · let us / let's [verb] · us [plural noun] in object position — for us researchers · institutional: how are we feeling?
entries.contrast: generic we differs from generic you and one by including the speaker explicitly and drafting the hearer — We need to talk about the deficit asserts a shared stake that One needs to pointedly does not. Four flavors are worth telling apart: the generic/inclusive we (we live in an age of…), the editorial or authorial we standing for a single writer, the royal we, and the institutional we of Are we ready for our shot?, which means you and is best avoided with adults. Case still applies when a noun follows: we researchers as subject, us researchers as object (for us researchers, ✗ for we researchers) — delete the noun and the right form is obvious. That deletion test is the same one that settles every coordination, and it is worth stating in full here because this is the entry where case comes up. Take the other person out and read what is left: He gave it to Bob and me → He gave it to me ✓; between you and me → between … me ✓, the preposition taking the object form as it always does; She and I went → I went ✓. Run backwards, it catches the plain error ✗ Me and him went (✗ Me went, ✗ Him went — the repair is He and I went, since the case is what is wrong and not the order) and the two hypercorrections that come from over-fixing it, ✗ between you and I and ✗ They invited my wife and I (✗ between … I, ✗ They invited … I). The second of those has no preposition anywhere in it: a coordinated direct object takes the object form for the same reason. See Case: the rule, the test, and where Americans actually break it.
entries.see also: you (generic), one (generic), they (generic), he (generic), we, us

entries.meaning: 'Anyone in this position' — the everyday American way of saying something is true of people generally.
examples: You can't get a decent apartment in that neighborhood anymore.
First you brown the onions, then you add the garlic.
It's the kind of noise you stop hearing after about a week.
You never know what a jury is going to do.
If you miss the last train, you're stuck downtown until morning.
You have to watch yourself on those stairs when they're icy.
They tax you on it whether you sell or not.

senses.head: People in general
body: You never know what a jury will do. 2. Instructional. Recipes, directions, and how-to prose: You take two eggs and you beat them until…
examples: You can't get a decent apartment in that neighborhood anymore.
First you brown the onions, then you add the garlic.

You never know what a jury is going to do.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /jə/ and /jʊ/; after /d/ or /t/ it fuses — did you [dɪdʒə], don't you [doʊntʃə], what do you think [wʌɾəjə ˈθɪŋk]
entries.русский: обобщённое ты/вы — «любой в такой ситуации»; по-русски чаще безличный оборот
entries.case: one form for subject and object; possessive determiner your, which is a determiner and is entered in the determiner dictionary; standalone possessive yours; reflexive yourself
entries.register: neutral — the ordinary American choice in speech and in most writing; some academic style guides and conservative editors still object
entries.person / number: second person in form; number is not marked at all. It takes plural verb forms like every you, but the singular reflexive yourself.
entries.refers to: people in general — "anyone in this position." There is no antecedent, and the actual addressee is not the point, though a reader may take it personally anyway.
entries.agreement: plural verb forms, always — you are, you have, you were — even for one generic person. ✗ you is, ✗ you was (nonstandard — the vernacular leveling of be, general in African American English and in Southern, Appalachian, and working-class white American speech, and you was was ordinary in eighteenth-century educated English before the prescriptivists drove it out). The reflexive is singular yourself (you have to watch yourself), because the reference is one person at a time.
entries.pattern: you [verb] · you can / have to / never [verb] · your [noun] · yourself · instructional: first you brown the onions · you know / you never know as fixed frames
entries.ambiguity: a reader can hear an accusation — You can't trust anyone in that department may land as a charge against the reader; the fixes are the passive, a plural noun (drivers, patients, researchers), or one.
entries.person shift: choose one generic and hold it — ✗ When one is tired, you make mistakes. Note also that generic you is neither singular nor plural, so the regional plurals are address forms, not generics, and each carries its own label: y'all is Southern and African American English and standard within those varieties, and it is spreading nationally; you guys is national and informal rather than nonstandard, and is under pressure for being gendered; youse is nonstandard, and belongs to New York City, northern New Jersey, Philadelphia, Boston, and Chicago; you'uns and yinz are nonstandard, Appalachian and Pittsburgh. None of the marked forms belongs in formal writing — write all of you, you all, or name the group.
entries.contrast: generic you is what Americans say where the British write one; one is formal, you is neutral, and generic they is for what unnamed others do. Two traps.
entries.see also: one (generic), we (generic), they (generic), he (generic), you, youse

entries.meaning: 'Me, with a wink' — the speaker in the third person, claiming the credit or the blame.
examples: Guess who got stuck cleaning up after all of them? Yours truly.
The only person in the building who had read the whole contract was yours truly.
They handed the entire mess to yours truly about ten minutes before the deadline.
Yours truly has been saying that for three years, for whatever it is worth. (third-person verb, first-person meaning)
If anything goes wrong on Saturday, it is yours truly they will be calling at six in the morning.
Photograph by yours truly, taken from the roof of the parking garage. (the credit line)
The letter still closes Yours truly, but that is the valediction it started as, not the pronoun.

senses.head: The punch line
body: Answering a question the speaker has just set up: And who do you suppose had to clean it all up? Yours truly. 2. The complaint. They handed the whole thing to yours truly at five o'clock on a Friday. 3. The credit line. Photograph by yours truly — one of the few places the phrase turns up in print rather than in speech.
examples: Guess who got stuck cleaning up after all of them? Yours truly.
The only person in the building who had read the whole contract was yours truly.
They handed the entire mess to yours truly about ten minutes before the deadline.
Yours truly has been saying that for three years, for whatever it is worth. (third-person verb, first-person meaning)
If anything goes wrong on Saturday, it is yours truly they will be calling at six in the morning.
Photograph by yours truly, taken from the roof of the parking garage. (the credit line)
The letter still closes Yours truly, but that is the valediction it started as, not the pronoun.

entries.pronunciation note: accent on tru-, with a secondary beat on yours; many Americans have /jʊrz/ for yours, and in fast speech the first word reduces to [jɚz], so the phrase runs to [jɚz ˈtruli]. The phrase as a whole has no weak form, because it almost always ends its sentence and takes the sentence accent — which is the whole point of reaching for it
entries.русский: шутл. ваш покорный слуга — только о самом говорящем; форма неизменяема
entries.case: none, and that is the tell — one invariant form does subject and object alike (Yours truly got stuck with the bill, They gave it to yours truly), which marks it as a fixed phrase rather than a pronoun with a paradigm; the possessive yours truly's exists as a further joke and is rare in print
entries.register: informal and always jocular. It is a wink — the speaker steps into the third person to take credit, lodge a complaint, or land a punch line — and it has no neutral use and no place in formal writing, where the word is I or me
entries.type: jocular first-person pronominal — a frozen letter closing pressed into service as a noun phrase meaning me
entries.person / number: first person singular in meaning, third person singular in grammar, and the mismatch is the joke.
entries.refers to: the speaker or writer, and nobody else, ever. It cannot be handed to a third party: ✗ Ask yours truly's brother said of somebody else's brother is not English.
entries.agreement: third-person singular verb — Yours truly is the one who has to explain this to the board, Yours truly was volunteered again. ✗ Yours truly am, which lets the meaning's person leak into the grammar. The follow-up pronouns stay in the third person as well, and sliding back into the first breaks the device: ✗ Yours truly, in my opinion, would go further.
entries.pattern: Yours truly [singular verb] · [verb] yours truly · [preposition] yours truly — to yours truly, for yours truly, by yours truly · the answer frame Who…? — Yours truly. · the credit line photograph by yours truly · the letter closing Yours truly, — the frozen original, and not this pronoun
entries.contrast: the phrase has two lives and only one of them belongs in this file. The letter closing Yours truly, is a valediction: it fills no noun slot, takes no verb, and is where the pronoun came from. The pronominal yours truly stands exactly where I or me would — Guess who got stuck cleaning up? Yours truly. Against the other devices for keeping I off the page, all of them entered nearby: the present writer is the scholar's, stiff and dated; the undersigned is the contract's; deponent is the affidavit's; the editorial we is one writer wearing a plural; and yours truly is the only one of the set that is meant to be funny. Two mechanics. No apostrophe, ever — yours is a possessive pronoun, and that family never takes one (✗ your's truly), a rule it shares with its, hers, ours, and theirs. And there is no plural: ✗ ours truly for a group is not available, and a speaker who wants the joke for two people has to build it some other way.
entries.see also: the present writer, the present author, deponent, affiant, we (generic), one (generic), yours, I, me, the undersigned

entries.meaning: Holds the object slot for a clause that has been pushed to the end of the sentence.
examples: I find it strange that nobody called the police.
She made it clear that the offer expires on Friday.
I'd appreciate it if you'd let me know either way.
He owes it to his family to at least try.
I hate it when the coffee shop closes early.
The board thought it best to postpone the vote.
I take it you've already heard.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ət/; before a vowel the t flaps, so find it odd runs to [ˈfaɪn əɾ ˈɑd]
entries.русский: формальное дополнение it — держит место придаточного, вынесенного в конец; не переводится
entries.case: object
entries.register: neutral
entries.person / number: third person singular, invariant. No gender, no plural.
entries.refers to: nothing — it holds the object slot open for a that-clause, when-clause, if-clause, or infinitive that has been moved to the end of the sentence. What it anticipates is a clause, never a noun.
entries.agreement: none — it is an object. The main verb agrees with the sentence's own subject.
entries.pattern: [subject] [verb] it [adjective] that [clause] — I find it odd that… · [subject] [verb] it [noun phrase] to [verb] — She considers it a waste to… · [subject] [verb] it when/if [clause] — I hate it when…, I'd appreciate it if… · [subject] owes/takes/leaves it [phrase] — He owes it to them to try, I take it that…
entries.contrast: with the verbs that require it, leaving the it out is an error, and it is one of the most frequent in nonnative writing: ✗ I find strange that he called, ✗ I'd appreciate if you would call, ✗ She considers a waste to argue about it. The working rule: it is obligatory when an adjective or noun phrase stands between the verb and the clause (find it odd that, make it clear that, think it best to, consider it a waste to), and after hate / like / love / appreciate / prefer + when or if. One honest exception, common enough that it has to be named: make clear, make plain, and make known have fossilized enough to stand without the it in edited American English — The court made clear that the rule applies is as good as made it clear that, and neither is a correction of the other. That is a property of those make idioms and of nothing else in the group: the find, consider, and appreciate patterns above still require their it. It is not used when the clause follows the verb directly: I know that he called, ✗ I know it that he called. Distinguish it from referential it, which points at a thing — in I found it odd the it is the situation to come, in I found it under the couch it is the wallet.
entries.see also: it (extraposition), it (cleft), it (idiomatic object), what (fused relative), it

entries.meaning: Splits a sentence in two to put one element under the spotlight.
examples: It was Maria who called, not her brother.
It's the humidity that gets to me, not the heat.
It wasn't until Thursday that anyone noticed the error.
It was the neighbors who complained about the noise.
Was it you who left the back door open?
It's not the falling that hurts; it's the landing.
It is in the second paragraph that the argument falls apart.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ət/; it was runs to [əɾ wəz] and it's to [əts]
entries.русский: формальное it в обороте It was X who… — выделение, рус. «именно X»; не переводится
entries.case: subject
entries.register: neutral — the cleft is ordinary in both speech and writing
entries.person / number: third person singular, invariant, and it stays singular even when the spotlighted element is plural.
entries.refers to: nothing. The cleft splits one clause in two so a single element can be spotlighted: Maria called becomes It was Maria who called.
entries.agreement: the copula agrees with the dummy, so it is singular whatever the focus — It was the neighbors who complained, ✗ It were the neighbors. The verb inside the cleft clause agrees with the focused element instead: It is I who am responsible (formal), It's the kids who are the problem.
entries.pattern: It + be + [focused noun phrase] + who/that [clause] · It + be + [focused adverbial] + that [clause] — It was on Tuesday that… · negative: It wasn't the money that bothered him · question: Was it Maria who called? · It wasn't until [time] that [clause]
entries.contrast: the cleft is also where the old case question gets settled. It was I who broke it is the formal nominative version; It's me is ordinary standard American English and has been for centuries — write It's me, not It is I, unless the register is deliberately elevated. That honesty has a limit, though: in a coordination the case is still decided by the slot the pronoun sits in, and the deletion test decides it — between you and me, They invited my wife and me, She and I went, against the error ✗ Me and him went and the hypercorrection ✗ between you and I (worked through at we (generic) and in full at Case). Inside the cleft clause, who is for people, which for things, and that for both — It was Maria who called and It was Maria that called are equally good — while whose covers people and things alike. And remember that the American preference for restrictive that over restrictive which is an editing convention, not a rule of grammar; the one hard rule there is that that cannot introduce a nonrestrictive clause. Against it (extraposition), the test is the gap: in a cleft the material after who/that is missing the focused element (It was Maria who called), while in extraposition the that-clause is complete (It is clear that she was right).
entries.see also: it (extraposition), it (anticipatory object), what (fused relative), who, that

entries.meaning: Holds the subject slot for a clause that has been moved to the end of the sentence.
examples: It is clear that nobody actually read the contract.
It's important to arrive at least an hour early.
It turns out the flight was canceled before we even left the house.
It bothers me that she never apologized.
It's no use complaining about it now.
It seems that the two departments never spoke to each other.
It has been decided that the office will close on Fridays.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ət/; it is runs to [ɪɾ ɪz], it's to [əts]
entries.русский: формальное подлежащее it — место придаточного-подлежащего, вынесенного в конец
entries.case: subject
entries.register: neutral — the default way to build these sentences
entries.person / number: third person singular, invariant.
entries.refers to: nothing on its own. It is a placeholder for a subject clause — a that-clause, an infinitive, or an -ing clause — that has been moved to the end because English prefers heavy material last.
entries.agreement: singular verb, always — It is clear that the numbers were wrong, ✗ It are clear. The verb stays singular no matter how many plurals the extraposed clause contains: It is obvious that the results were fabricated.
entries.pattern: It [be] [adjective] that [clause] · It [be] [noun phrase] to [verb] · It [verb] [object] that [clause] — It bothers me that… · It seems / appears / turns out / happens that… · It's no use [verb-ing] · It is said / believed / thought that… — the impersonal passive
entries.contrast: the unextraposed version is grammatical but almost never chosen: That she was right is clear against It is clear that she was right. What is not available is dropping the subject — ✗ Is clear that she was right — the standard interference error for speakers of Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Polish, and Russian. Against it (cleft): here the that-clause is complete, while a cleft leaves a gap where the focused element belongs. Against existential there: it introduces a proposition, there introduces the existence of a thing — It is a problem that nobody checked versus There is a problem. This construction is also the polite formal substitute for generic they: They say the bridge will close → It is said that the bridge will close.
entries.see also: it (cleft), it (anticipatory object), there (existential), they (generic), what (fused relative)

entries.meaning: A meaningless it welded into a fixed expression, where no noun could ever stand.
examples: We barely made it to the gate before they closed the door.
Knock it off — people are trying to work.
He's been lording it over the rest of the team since the promotion.
Let's call it a day and pick this up tomorrow.
They roughed it for a week with no hot water.
I hadn't prepared anything, so I just winged it.
We're going to have to tough it out until payday.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ət/; in these idioms it is unstressed and the verb or particle carries the accent — knock it off [ˈnɑk əɾ ˈɔf]
entries.русский: it в устойчивых оборотах (make it, hoof it) — часть идиомы, отдельно не переводится
entries.case: object
entries.register: informal to neutral, depending on the idiom
entries.person / number: third person singular, invariant, and frozen — it cannot be pluralized, questioned, replaced by a noun, or promoted to subject by a passive.
entries.refers to: nothing at all. The it is part of the idiom's spelling, not a pronoun with a job.
entries.agreement: none.
entries.pattern: [verb] it — make it, wing it, rough it, cool it, beat it · [verb] it [particle] — knock it off, hash it out, tough it out, live it up · [verb] it [preposition] [object] — lord it over someone, have it out with someone · [verb] it [noun] — call it a day, call it quits
entries.contrast: the test that separates this it from referential it is whether a what-question can reach it. He fixed it invites "Fixed what?" — referential. He made it, meaning he arrived or survived or succeeded, has no answer to "Made what?" — idiomatic. Because the it is frozen, the idiom will not passivize or pluralize: ✗ It was made by him in the "arrived" sense, ✗ They lorded them over us. And the spelling trap runs through every one of these: its is the possessive, it's is it is or it has. If you can expand it to it is, it takes the apostrophe.

entries.meaning: Fills the subject slot for the weather, the clock, the calendar, and the space around you.
examples: It's been raining since Thursday afternoon.
What time is it? — It's almost quarter to six.
It's only about twenty minutes from here if the traffic cooperates.
It gets dark around five o'clock in December.
It was ninety-four degrees on the tarmac when we landed.
It's freezing in this office.
It's Tuesday, so the trash goes out tonight.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /ət/; it's is [əts], and in very casual speech the vowel drops out altogether — it's raining [ts ˈreɪnɪŋ]
entries.русский: безличное it: о погоде, времени, расстоянии — в русском подлежащего нет вовсе
entries.case: subject
entries.register: neutral
entries.person / number: third person singular, invariant.
entries.refers to: nothing — there is no answer to "what is raining?" This it covers the weather, the clock, the calendar, the temperature, a distance, a duration, and the general state of the surroundings, none of which the sentence has named.
entries.agreement: singular verb, always — It is, It was, It gets, It has been. ✗ It are.
entries.pattern: It [be] [weather adjective] — It's cold · It [be] [verb-ing] — It's snowing · It [be] [clock time / day / date] — It's ten after four, It's Tuesday · It [be] [distance or duration] to/from [place] — It's three miles to the airport · It [verb] — It rained all night, It gets dark by five
entries.contrast: this is the hardest dummy for speakers of languages that drop the subject or build these sentences with a possession verb. English demands the pronoun (✗ Is raining, ✗ Rains a lot here), and it demands it specifically — not there and not have: ✗ There is raining, ✗ It has three miles to the airport, ✗ There are three miles to the airport (compare Spanish hay, French il y a). Existential there asserts that a thing exists, so There's a storm coming is fine because a storm is a noun, while It is storming describes the ambient condition with no noun at all. The minimal pair to remember is It's windy against There's a strong wind.

entries.meaning: Announces that something exists or is present, holding the subject slot while the real subject waits its turn.
examples: There's a message for you on the machine.
There are three good reasons not to sign this.
There was nobody at the desk when I came in.
Is there any coffee left?
There must be a simpler way to do this.
There used to be a hardware store on that corner.
There were fewer complaints this quarter than last.
There's a lot to talk about, isn't there?
entries.pronunciation note: existential there is nearly always weak — /ðɚ/, so there are two runs to [ðɚ ɚ ˈtu] and there's to [ðɚz]. The strong /ðɛr/ belongs to the locative adverb; if you hear a full vowel, the word means "in that place"
entries.русский: оборот there is/are — «есть, имеется, существует»; места не обозначает
entries.case: subject
entries.register: neutral
entries.person / number: none of its own — it borrows both from the noun phrase that follows the verb.
entries.refers to: nothing, and in particular not to a place. It exists so the sentence can announce that something exists or is present, with the real subject postponed until after the verb.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the noun phrase that follows, not with there — There is a problem, There are problems, There was one applicant, There were three applicants. Two honest qualifications: before a coordinated list the verb almost always matches the first noun (There is a fork and two knives on the table), and before an amount treated as a single block it is singular (There is ten dollars in the drawer).
entries.pattern: There [be] [indefinite noun phrase] ([place or time phrase]) · There [be] [noun phrase] to [verb] — There's a lot to do · There [modal] be [noun phrase] — There must be a reason · formal, with other verbs: There arose, There remains, There exists, There seems to be · question: Is there…?, Are there any…? · tag: There's a problem, isn't there?
entries.nonstandard: negative concord in the existential — There ain't nobody home, There wasn't nothing we could do — is systematic and rule-governed in African American English and in Southern, Appalachian, and working-class vernacular speech, and it was ordinary English before the eighteenth century; it is nevertheless nonstandard in edited American English, which allows one negative per clause: There isn't anybody home, There was nothing we could do. See nothing (negative concord).
entries.contrast: existential there against locative there — both can appear in one sentence, which settles it: There's a bus stop there. The first is unstressed and means nothing; the second is stressed and means "at that spot." Against dummy it: there asserts existence, it describes an ambient condition or identifies something — There is a problem introduces the problem, It is a problem comments on something already in view. The noun after existential there is normally indefinite, which is why ✗ There is my wallet on the table is wrong as an existential (rewrite as My wallet is on the table) and only works if you are pointing, in which case there is the locative. The tag question is the proof that this there is a real grammatical subject — the tag copies it the way it would copy any subject: There were no messages, were there?
entries.see also: there's, there're, it (weather, time, and distance), it (extraposition), their

entries.meaning: The contracted existential — the form the construction actually takes in speech, agreement problems and all.
examples: There's a package for you by the front door.
There've been three complaints about that intersection this month.
There'll be plenty of time to talk about it after dinner.
There're a few things we should go over first.
There's two things I want to say before we start. (ordinary speech; edited to there are)
There'd been no warning at all before the layoffs.
entries.pronunciation note: there're /ˈðɛrɚ/ collapses in ordinary speech to [ðɛɚ] or plain [ðɛr], barely distinguishable from there alone — one reason it is so rarely written. Also there've /ðɛrv/, there'll /ðɛrl/, there'd /ðɛrd/
entries.русский: стяжённые there is / there are — «есть, имеется»; разг.
entries.case: subject
entries.register: informal to neutral in speech; there's before a plural is informal in writing
entries.person / number: there's contracts a singular verb (there is, there has); there're contracts a plural one (there are).
entries.refers to: nothing — see there (existential).
entries.agreement: this is the whole point of the entry. In edited writing the verb must match the following noun: There's a problem / There are problems. In speech, there's before a plural is near-universal at every level of American English — there's two things I want to say, there's a lot of people here — and it is best understood as a fixed opener rather than an agreement decision made in real time. It is still marked as an error in edited prose, and a conservative editor will change every instance. There're is grammatically correct but awkward to say and rare on paper; most writers use the full there are.
entries.pattern: There's [singular noun phrase] · There're [plural noun phrase] · There've been [plural noun phrase] · There'll be [noun phrase] · There'd been [noun phrase] · spoken only: There's [plural noun phrase]
entries.contrast: keep there's apart from theirs and from the homophone set. The apostrophe in there's marks the missing letter of is or has; theirs, being a possessive pronoun, never takes one. In the three-way there / their / they're, there is the place or the dummy, their is the possessive determiner, they're is they are — and in the existential frame only there is possible: ✗ Their's a problem, ✗ They're are two options.
entries.see also: there (existential), they (generic), it (weather, time, and distance), their
